speechtext: Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 40) to amend the Criminal Act respecting homicide while hunting. He said:	The Bill is similar to the one I introduced Some two sessions ago. Since then the necessity for the legislation has become greater. During last fall's hunting season, 113 persons were killed in the states bordering on Canada and 94 injured. In my opinion, since homicide is a crime, the man who, while indulging in the sport and pleasure of hunting, does not take sufficient precaution to make sure that what he is shooting at is not a human being, should be punished when his lack of care leads to the loss of human life or injury. The man who does not give the benefit of the doubt to a human being, when he is not quite certain that what he is aiming at is a wild

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: animal, and who, through his neglect, kills or injures a fellow man is a criminal. The poor trapper or habitant who shoots a deer by mistake which turns out to be a cow moose, has his goods and chattels taken from him; but if it be a human being that he has shot by mistake, he is allowed to go free without even a preliminary investigation. I ask that this Bill and others of a similar nature should be referred to a committee. I do not say that the Bill is one which will cover all the circumstances that may arise, but I do urge that the matter should be taken up by a committee of legal and expert men, and I have no doubt that they will succeed in devising a measure which will cover the case.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time.

Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 41) respecting wireless telegraphy on ships. He said: "The Bill is modelled almost exactly on the one I introduced last year and which was sent to a committee. But the committee, while in favour of the principle of the Bill, thought it was premature. The circumstances now, however, are more imperative and demand that we should have a law of this kind. The United States government and the Canadian government have instituted wireless .telegraph stations all over the lakes and on the eastern and western sea-boards. It is possible that this Bill, which is modelled on the English measure, may not suit the circumstances and exigencies in this country, but I ask that it be referred to a committee of marine men who will draft a measure acceptable to all parties. I have in my hand an account of a large number of cases within the last two years in which this mysterious and invisible agency called from the deep the assistance of men. I refer to the 'Republic,' off the coast of New York, thp ' Ohio,' off the coast of Alaska, and also on August 11, 1910, to a ship which was on fire in Lake Michigan, all which made their predicament known by the wireless. Then there was the rudderless Clyde liner ' Iroquois ' which drifted about helpless until rescued through help summoned by the wireless. Let me read this despatch from the city of Chicago:
Chicago, March 29.-Passenger steamers on the Great Lakes are to be equipped this season with wireless telegraph apparatus to be operated by the United Wireless Telegraph Company. Contracts were closed here to-day with the steamship companies, and stations have been established to be ready by the opening of navigation at Chicago, Detroit, the Soo, Mackinac and all the principal lake ports.
Every passenger boat, capable of carrying more than fifty passengers should be equip-

ped with this wonderful agency for the preservation of human life.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Mines) moved that the House go into committee on Tuesday next to consider the following proposed resolution:-
Resolved, that it is expedient (a) to regulate the manufacture, importation, storage, handling, testing and use of explosive material of every description ; (b) to grant licenses to factories and magazines for the manufacture and storage of explosives and to provide for the inspection thereof and the payment of fees for such licenses; (c) to make inquiries into the cause of explosions, and of accidents caused by explosives; (d) to provide for the appointment of inspectors and other officers required for the administration of the Act, and the payment of the salaries thereof; (e) to authorize the Governor in Council to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the Act; and (f) to provide for the imposition of penalties in contravention thereof.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been informed of the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.

I desire to say a few words on the subject of questions asked and answered in the House and the way in which the new rule concerning them is being interpreted. There are two points to which I wish to refer. In the first place, answers to questions appeared in ' Hansard ' on Wednesday last in two places. Those answered orally appeared in the first part of ' Hansard ' in the place in which answers to questions always appear; those answered in writing are at the end of ' Hansard.' It seems to me that it would be far better if these answers to questions, whether made orally or in writing, appeared in order in one part of ' Hansard,' as they have always done. The second point is that on Friday last certain questions were answered in writing, and, of course, under the method adopted, they appeared at the end of ' Hansard.' I submit that it would be far better if we had the written answers to questions appearing only on those days on which we reach questions in customary order on the Order Paper. That is, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, questions are the first order on the Paper, and we naturally look for them on those days. Answers put in writing do not appear in ' Hansard ' in the order in which they were on the Order
Paper. The rule has not been altered, except that certain questions are allowed to be answered in writing and not orally, and I submit that the intention of the rule as worded is that the answers to questions should appear in ' Hansard ' exactly the same as they always have done, and also that whether given orally or in writing they should appear in the order in which they stand on the Order Paper. The object of the new rule, as I understand it, was purely to save time. In order to make that rule welcome to the members of the House it must be made as easy and convenient as possible. Members have always been in the habit of looking at the first part of ' Hansard ' of Monday, Wednesday and Thursday for answers to questions, and the answers should appear on those days, as they have always done. And they should not be printed in ' Hansard ' in the order in which the written answers happen to come in, but in the order given on the Order Paper. Thus, for instance, if I have a question numbered 16 on the Order Paper, I ought to be able to learn, by looking at the relative place in ' Hansard ' whether it has been answered or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I interpret the rule exactly as my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) does, and think that if his suggestions are followed great confusion will be avoided.
I. would suggest, also, that when a question is answered in writing, a copy should be sent to the gentleman who asks the question, and also a copy laid on the table.

My recollection is otherwise.
And I added that I would look into the matter, which is not recorded. Now, it was a very notable occasion on which this matter referred to came up. It says there that an argument intervened and as it is of importance to show that this was no ordinary occasion, that it was an occasion which, unless a gentleman was peculiarly indifferent to insinuations against his honour as a professional man and as a public man, he would be likely to remember, I shall read from the Montreal ' Herald ', a Liberal newspaper :

Ottawa, Feby. 1.-Last evening's session of the Public Accounts Committee was one of the stormiest in recent years, and sometimes the babel was so great, half a dozen members endeavouring to speak simultaneously, that the chairman, Mr. Carvell, had great difficulty in preserving order.
Then it points out that certain dredging contracts were np in the earlier part of the evening and the report proceeds :
Sub-targets again.

Then follows further discussion and then comes the ruling that was spoken of so often the other day, and so well described by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Smyth) :
Compliance with rules of evidence was insisted on, backed by the Minister of Public Works, and discussion of this point took up nearly an hour. Mr. Haughton Lennox remarked that the people were beginning to think there were too many lawyers in parliament.

I quite agree with that statement, but there are lawyers and lawyers.

And, before I have finished the reading of this, I shall point out that there is quite a distinction between lawyers and lawyers, and if hon. gentlemen on that side of the House can produce a farmer in the House of Commons who has more consistently and strenuously advocated the interests of the farming class than I have-

' According to his own statement , that is not exactly according to the record, but it suits my point all right. v

I do not think the minister will ask what it means.
Hear, hear.

Although I am a lawyer, trot him out right away. The report .proceeds :
The policy of the lawyers on the Liberal side was to stifle investigation.
What about that for a class of lawyers? That is one of the distinctions.

That was a remark of the hon. gentleman, myself, and I could not get the ruling of the Chair in my favour on that point any more than on any others.
I do not wonder at that.
But I think I will get a ruling of the public on that in my favour.
They did not say that in October, 1908, by their votes.

When I came to parliament I had a majority of 800. The next election I had a majority of something over 800. Then the county was gerrymandered and I was cut out of 400 votes by the gerrymander, yet I obtained a majority of about 1,500. The report proceeds :
In the course of the discussion Mr. Pugsley referred to Mr. Lennox.

That is the way in which it is put by the reform journal. I looked up the columns of the ' Globe ' and the ' Globe ' is much to the same effect, although it hands out bouquets to the Minister of Public Works and damns the Conservatives as usual. Then, to show something of what actually happened, I will take a still



more reliable authority, the ' Mail and Empire and after that I will close. I want to point to this fact that if the minister has a memory on which he prides himself, it is singular that he did not give us the benefit of his memory the other day, honestly and candidly, because the discussion that went on that day in the committee was not such as to slip from the memory of a sensitive man.
STORMY SCENES IN COMMITTEE. Liberal Lawyers again resort to Obstruction Tactics.-Mr. Pugsley levels insult-Receives a retort that makes him wince- Sub-target Gun Contract under the Searchlight.
Ottawa, January 31.-The obstructive tactics of the Liberal lawyers, who are members of the Public Accounts Committee, in seeking to throttle inquiry into scandals connected with the management of government departments, this morning led to one of the most extraordinary and wildest scenes which ever took place before a committee of the House of Commons. At times the meeting was in a perfect uproar, a dozen members were on their feet at one time, shouting angrily across the room, whilst personalities of a particularly pointed character were freely exchanged. The Minister of Public Works and the exMinister of Railways were the subjects of two particularly cutting retorts.
The minister forgot.
A new feature in connection with the conduct of the proceedings was the fact which is now becoming apparent that Mr. Macdonald and Mr. MacLean, the Liberal members for Pictou and Lunenburg, respectively, are no longer to fulfil alone the role of arch-obstructionists. To-day Hon. Wm. Pugsley, Minister of Public Works, ex-Minister of Railways Emmerson, Honore Gervais, the French Liberal member for the St. James division of Montreal, came to the assistance of the other two, and between them they succeeded by their trivial objections in preventing evidence being taken.
Passing over a good deal of discussion that is recorded here, I find these sentences also, and this is a more correct version of what happened than even that which appears in the ' Herald,' as will be remembered by the gentlemen who were in the committee on that occasion.

The discussion was getting more and more heated, but it was when Mr. Haughton Lennox, of South Simcoe, rose to demand fair play and to protest against the absurd objections raised by the legal stalwarts of the government, that the storm really burst. I am a lawyer myself, he remarked, and I say that there is a growing feeling in the country that there are too many lawyers in this House and on this committee.
A harmless remark that I made, casually referring to the fact that I was a lawyer and yet I could see that there were too Mr. LENNOX.
many lawyers in the House, but it was this that brought down the thunder of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works and the insult that has been referred to.
' It's the same in any country in the world/ interrupted Mr. Gervais in broken English.
Warming to his subject, Mr. Lennox proceeded amidst much disorder and frequent interruptions to complain of the unfair tactics of the government supporters. He repeated that there were too many lawyers on the committee, and asserted that they came there simply to block investigation. While Mr. Lennox was still on his feet, Mr. Gervais rose and attempted to address the meeting but his voice was drowned by the laughter and shouts of the members.
Does it say that Mr. Gervais' voice was drowned by laughter?
Yes.
Who was guilty of the laughter?

I do not think any body was guilty, but I think it was our side that laughed. Now I come to what Mr. Gervais said:
Mr. Gervais went on to harangue the meeting. Acting Chairman Carvell was absolutely powerless, and the whole exhibition which Mr. Gervais was making became absolutely ludicrous. The meeting was convulsed. [DOT] When the Montreal member had subsided, Mr. Lennox remarked: ' Its because the gentlemen are hit that they will not keep quiet/
' I have never been hit by anybody/ exclaimed Mr. Gervais excitedly, and there was another outburst of laughter.
Mr. Lennox stuck to his guns and once more amidst intense disorder repeated his statement about the lawyers and their efforts to block investigation.
Now Mr. Pugsley.
Mr. Pugsley, in a brief period of space, explained what he considered should be admitted as evidence, and in the course of his remarks, cast a gratuitous insult at Mr. Lennox by saying: 'Mr. Lennox is a lawyer-so he tells us.'
So he tells us.
The Liberal members laughed, but Mr. Lennox waited until Mr. Pugsley had finished, and then made the Minister of Public Works wince with the following retort: 'The minister says I tell them I am a lawyer. I will one day take the opportunity of showing him that I am not only a lawyer, but I stand true to my clients/ (Uproar.)
Mr. Pugsley, to whom this remark was directly addressed, exclaimed: 'I think the hon. member should explain.'
Member struck below belt.
'I will explain nothing/ Mr. Lennox answered fiercely.
Answers fiercely!
Fiercely, it says. I think I am always very mild.
And yet that is in the ' Mail and Empire

Oh, yes, but they probably misunderstood my manner. However, I am willing to let that go.
'The minister strikes below the belt when he says the contemptible thing' he said a minute ago.' (Renewed disorder.)
1 made another remark on that occasion which was drowned in the disorder, and I do not think I need repeat it here. The minister who prides himself upon his memory questioned my position the other day, and made statements during the debate that did not at all agree with my memory of what had occurred. The minister may have a memory as good as he likes, hut the better his memory the less is it to his credit that he made such a statement the other day, because there are worse things to be possessed of than a bad memory. I have said all that is necessary upon this occasion, I say it with distinct emphasis because I have noticed the attitude that the minister has taken in many discussions in the House in which some personalities have been introduced, but this was not a personal attack and therefore I could not raise the question of privilege.
Am I permitted, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words in reply to the hon. gentleman?
It is a personal explanation, I take it?

With your permission, Sir, I will do so. I think the official record of what took place before the Committee on Public Accounts confirms very strongly the statement which I made. It will be remembered that the hon. gentleman made the charge that I had taken part in obstructing an investigation of dhe subtarget gun case. I entirely repudiated that statement. I said that I had not in any way blocked the investigation and that' I had no recollection of being present. Now, I may say to my hon. friend, whether he chooses to believe me or not, that in making that statement I was perfectly sincere. I had no recollection of being present at an inquiry with reference to the sub-target gun, and my reason was that I have made a practice of not attending meetings of the Public Accounts Committee unless there is some matter up for investigation in connection with my own department, and then only in cases where the deputy minister informs me that my presence is required with respect to some special matter. Now, it appears that on that occasion to which my hon. friend refers the matter of dredging contracts had been up for consideration before the committee at that very sitting, 32i
and that was the reason why I was present, and not because there was any investigation of the question of sub-target guns. Now, I appeal to you whether anything that my hon. friend has read, even from the * Mail and Empire ', shows that I sought to obstruct the proceedings of the committee. It appears that I never said a word until after the chairman had given his decision, and then there appears to have been an uproar in the committee caused apparently by the fierce attitude of my hon. friend. Even the ' Mail ' says that he spoke fiercely, and when my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) who is usually so calm and moderate, gets so angry as to impress the reporter of the * Mail ' that he was fierce, there must have been something in it. The hon. gentleman admits that after the decision of the chairman, when Mr. Gervais was proceeding to make an argument, the gentlemen who are associated with my hon. friend tried to drown his voice with laughter. That must have been very rude; it must have been inexcusable, and I am surprised that my hon. friend should have been guilty of conduct of that kind. All I appear to have done was to insist as far as I could that this bear garden, which had evidently been brought into being by my hon. friend and others who were assisting him
Order.
I think that is all right.
Order.
Is that objected to?
It was a bear garden all right, but it was not brought into existence by my friends or by me.

According to the report of the ' Mail and Empire,' my hon. friend and his associates would seem to have brought that bear garden into existence, and I being present-because the dredging contracts had been under discussion-thought that I was simply doing my duty in endeavouring to put an end to that bear garden, which certainly was not creditable to the committee or to those who took part in it.

Certainly, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) was present.

Relying upon his exceedingly good memory, would the minister state to the House now whether he made that motion for the purpose of putting an end to the bear garden or for the sake of getting rid of my motion?
999	'
I do not pretend to remember all that took place three years ago; I have something more important to attend to and to think of.
Read the official report.

Mr. Chairman, it has been moved by Mr. Poster, seconded by Mr. Northrup, that the questions submitted to the witness and the decision with regard thereto, and the reasons given by the chair, and the appeal from the chair's decision be referred to the House forthwith.
Then an argument followed, and I do not remember that my hon. friend read anything which showed that I even took part in the argument.
It says so.
Well, it must have been a very moderate part.
It says that you took a very ' bland ' part.

Then the uproar took place, and I moved, seconded by Mr. Ger-vais that the meeting adjourn, and that the subject be discussed at a later sitting. I think, if the committee was in an uproar and if hon. gentlemen opposite were laughing at and ridiculing speakers as they were ridiculing Mr. Gervais, and as it wTas after one o'clock, and as the meeting had turned really into a bear garden, that it was not at all improper that I should move that the meeting adjourn, and that when, gentlemen opposite calmed down at a later sitting the matter might be considered. It does seem to me that my hon. friend has not made any point by bringing up this really unimportant matter. Let me say one word with regard to my hon. friend, whose relations to myself I would like to have as cordial as possible. The hon. gentleman thinks-and this appears to have been rankling in his bosom for some three years-that I insulted him upon that occasion, when I made the statement that he was a lawyer of repute and in his own estimation he was a good lawyer. That is about what I appear to have said. My hon. friend ought not to be insulted at that, because I presume that in the course of his life he has had many similar testimonials borne to his ability and experience as a lawyer.

It is not on record in the department, not that I have been able to find.

I bring to the attention of the Minister cf Militia a matter concerning which I have already spoken to him and which he suggested I should mention when the Militia department is under investigation. However, as straws show how the wind blows,
I consider it advisable to call his attention to the matter now. I do not think for a moment that the Minister of Militia is cognizant of, or has authorized the proceeding of which I am about to complain, because it is contrary to the democratic principles which in this country should prevail. It is in reference to a letter which I received last evening from the Department of Militia and Defence, with regard to members or other people who may have business with the department, the simplest way to bring the matter to the minister's attention is to read the letter:-
Department of Militia and Defence.
Ottawa, November 17, 1910. Dear Sir,-I am directed by the honourable the Minister to inclose a copy of regulations which have recently been passed, governing the admission of visitors to the Department of Militia and Defence during office hours, and which it is the intention to put into force on the 1st proximo, and to inclose, for your use, in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 2 of the regulations, a permanent pass for admission.
For many years a great deal of annoyance and interference with the public duties of the officials of the department have been caused by the unrestricted opportunities afforded the outside public to visit the employees upon private and personal matters and questions entirely foreign to the official duties imposed upon the working staff of the department, whose whole time belongs to the public. Although some care has been taken to protect the officials of the. department, yet it has been found impossible to check, to any reasonable degree, the annoyance indicated above.
Money lenders, promoters, agents and canvassers of all kinds seem to easily find their way to the officials high and low.
These regulations have, therefore, been framed in order to permit the officials and
employees of the department to perform their duties without unnecessary interruption. They will prove no barrier to those having official relations with the department.
I may add that these regulations are based upon regulations in force in the War Office, London, England.
Yours very truly,

Deputy Minister, Militia and Defence.
The first of the regulations refers to employees of the department. The second, third and fourth are as follow:
2.	In addition to the civil and military staff employed at headquarters, permanent passes will be issued to the following:-Senators, members of parliament, one representative of each newspaper, and officials of other departments (the deputy minister of each department to forward a list of those officials of his department to whom he wishes the privilege extended).
3.	To all others desirous of visiting the department, temporary passes will be issued, which must be given up on leaving.
4.	A visitor will note on the temporary pass, his name, address, nature of inquiry, and name of official with whom an interview is desired. The pass will then be taken up to the officer or official concerned, who, if he desires to see the visitor, will initial the pass, and the visitor will then be shown up to him. After the interview is ended, the officer or official concerned must see that his visitor is attended to the. exit by a messenger.
The seventh and eighth are as follow:
7.	Officers, officials and other persons employed in the department will, on appointment to the department, be furnished by the deputy minister with a permanent pass.
8.	Officers, officials and other persons employed in the department shall, on vacating their appointments, return their passes to the deputy minister.
There are other rules in reference to closing the doors.
Do people have to take their hats off when they go in?

I do not see any reference to that in the rules. The crux of the whole matter is in the last clause of the letter, which is as follows: ' I may add that these regulations are based upon regulations in force in the War Office, London, England.' Now, Sir, I strongly oppose, and I believe I shall always strongly oppose, unless circumstances materially change, the importation into this country of regular militarism. I back up the Minister of Militia in his intentions with reference to our militia service. If his ideas were carried out, I believe that service would be much improved. We are spending $7,000,000 on the militia, and what is the result? We have a frame, with nothing inside of it. In my young days in my home town there were three companies of militia who drilled weekly in the summer evenings, and vied

with each other for the higher skill. Now it is difficult in the same town to get half a company to attend the annual camp. The hands of the Minister of Militia are bound down by the militia council, on which there are some military gentlemen from the old land who look at all matters from a purely military point of view. But we are here to look matters from a practical point of view. I have read the statutes and I can see no reason or authority why a colonial officer, when appointed, not to the militia, but to the regular force of any colony, should nine times out of ten lose his practical common sense. In the old country they are bound down with red tape. We do not want that sort of thing here. What happened in my own case? One morning I wanted to consult an official in the Militia Department building, and I was told that the department was in the Woods building. I went there at about half-past ten. The guard at the door or the man at the elevator knew nothing * of the official I wanted. I went through almost every part of the building, and nobody seemed to know where he was. I found almost every official reading the Ottawa ' Morning Citizen '. Nobody seemed to want to be interrupted. I went again at half past two, with the same result. I could get no information, but this time they were reading ' Hansard '. I contend that we should not send ' Hansard ' to the civil servants of this country in office hours. I ask the minister to look into this matter. Why, Sir, I can consult the one man who has more power than the head of any other country in the world, that is,.the Prime Minister of Canada. I can have access to him at any time if in my proper order. I can consult any other minister of the Crown of the Dominion of Canada if I go in the proper sequence. So can any other free citizen of Canada. I mention these rules with the fullest confidence that the minister will take the facts in the spirit in which they are mentioned, for the good of Canada. I wish to back him up in every effort he makes for the improvement of the militia. While I am against regular militarism in this country, as are nine out of every ten Canadians in every province, still I think our young men instead of being in questionable places should learn to shoot and should drill during the summer evenings, as they formerly did when we spent $1,500,000 instead of $8,000,000 on the militia.
Would the hon. minister give both the letter and the circular into * Hansard ' and the House will dispense with his reading them?

It is the deputy minister who addressed this letter-not the General Officer Commanding, not the militia council-but the deputy minister. It is not an order of the militia council, as my hon. friend seems to think, and to which he takes some exception, but an order pure and simple of the official who is permanently at the head of the administration of the militia department. This is the letter:-
Department of Militia and Defence.
Ottawa, November 17, 1910. Dear Sir,-I am directed by the honourable the Minister to inclose a copy of regulations which have recently been passed, governing the admission of visitors to the Department of Militia and Defence during office hours, and which it is the intention to put into force on the 1st proximo, and to inclose, for your use, in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 2 of the regulations, a permanent pass for admission.
Eor many years a great deal of annoyance and interference with the public duties of the officials of the department have been caused by the unrestricted opportunities afforded the outside public to visit the employees upon private and personal matters and questions entirely foreign to the official duties imposed upon the working staff of the department, whose whole time belongs to the public. Although some care has been taken to protect the officials of the department, yet it has been found impossible to check, to any reasonable degree, the annoyances indicated above.
Money lenders, promoters, agents and canvassers of all kinds seem to easily find their way to the officials high and low.
These regulations have, therefore, been framed in order to permit the officials and employees of the department to perform their duties without unnecessary interruption. They will prove no barrier to those having official relations with the department.
I may add that these regulations are based upon regulations in force in the War Office, London, England.
Yours very truly,
EUG. EISET, [DOT]
Deputy Minister, Militia and Defence.
Now, the regulations which, I understand, my hon. friend would like to have read, are as follows:
Regulations governing the admission of visitors to the Department of Militia and Defence.
1.	Every officer, official or person employed in the department is liable to be challenged on entering or leaving and required to prove his indentity. Eor this purpose, permanent passes will be issued to every one concerned, and these passes must be produced at any time if called for by the orderlies who will be stationed at the entrance.
2.	In addition to the civil and military staff employed at headquarters, permanent passes will be issued to the following:-Senators, members of parliament, one representative of each newspaper, and officials of other departments (the deputy minister of each department to forward a list of those officials of his department to whom he wishes the privilege extended).
3.	To all others desirous of visiting the department, temporary passes will be issued, which must be given up on leaving.
4.	A visitor will note on the temporary pass, his name, address, nature of inquiry, and name of official with whom an interview is desired. The pass will then be taken up to the officer or official concerned, who, if he desires to see the visitor, will initial the pass,

and the visitor will then he shown up to him. After the interview is ended, the officer or official concerned must see that his visitor is attended to the exit by a messenger.
My hon. friend rather took exception to that. I think it is only fair that a visitor should be shown the way out as well as the way in.
5.	When visitors with temporary passes have been admitted to see an officer or official, and are referred by him to some other officer or official, or wish themselves to have a further interview elsewhere, the officer or official who first receives them is responsible for seeing that they are attended by a messenger.
6.	Civilian officials below the rank of Division II A, and non-commissioned officers and men, will not be permitted to see visitors except in cases of extreme urgency, in which event, however, the permission of the head of the branch or division must first be obtained.
7.	Officers, officials and other persons employed in the department will, on appointment to the department, be furnished by the deputy minister with a permanent pass.
8.	Officers, officials and other persons employed in the department shall, on vacating their appointments, return their passes to the deputy minister.
9.	Visitors, other than those holding permanent passes, shall only be admitted between the hours of 10.30 a.m. and 1 p.m. except by appointment.
10.	The doors leading into the Department of Militia and Defence on the east side will be closed at 5 p.m every week day except Saturday, when the hour of closing will be one o'clock p.m. Any person desiring admission to the department after those hours must use the west entrance, and upon showing to
_ the policeman on duty his permanent pass,
" and furnishing satisfactory proof as to his right to enter the building after office hours, will be admitted by that officer.

Colonel,
Deputy Minister, Militia and Defence. Department of Militia and Defence,
Ottawa, November 17, 1910.
I have only to say that I am glad my hon. friend (Mr. Lewis) has brought this question up, as it gives me an opportunity of explaining the real object had in view. There is no intention, no desire, to exclude anybody. I only wish that a great many more members of parliament would come to the department than do come. The door is open for them, and we are glad to see them at all times. As to the facility of getting into the department-or any of the departments-as compared with the conditions in other countries, I think I know something about these conditions in England and in the United States, and I can assure my hon. friend that there is no such liberty, if I may use the word-' license,' perhaps, would be better-of entering the corridor of the public departments and wandering from office to office as there is here in Ottawa. Any man who has business with

a department in the United States can enter that department, but he must make his way through the proper channel. I believe it would be infinitely better, in the interest of the public service if some such restrictions as are in force in the United States were in force here. I have endeavoured to make a commencement. As I have said, these regulations are probably far from perfect. I shall be glad if any hon. member of this House will give me any suggestions which will enable us to improve them.

As one who has looked into this matter considerably, I may be permitted to express my views upon it. I heartily approve the desire expressed by the minister (Sir Frederick Borden) in the memorandum, to keep out canvassers, hawkers, beggars and all that class of public nuisances that too frequently infest not only the corridors of the Militia Department, but also the precincts of parliament. But it is just a question whether, in endeavouring to carry out that design, a little injustice may not be done to those who wish to enfer the department on legitimate business. But the rules as explained by the minister, I think, are free from serious objection on that score. And what the minister says is true, it should not be necessary for a caller to ramble from room to room trying to find the officer wanted; there should be a clerk or officer at the door who can direct the visitor to the room of the person whom he desires to see. I presume that that is what the minister wishes. But there is another aspect of the case. Under these regulations, members of parliament are furnished with cards. When I received the notification,
I drew attention of the deputy minister to the fact that there is no door of the public service of the Dominion of Canada closed to a member of parliament. As one representing a riding in this House, I am, to that extent, a trustee of the public property here. I do not recognize that there is any door in any public service closed to a member of parliament in connection with his duties as a member. I know the minister will take that view of it.

Hear, hear. Mr. HUGHES. As to having the pass, it is the duty of the gentlemen who guard the doors to come up and look at the goodlooking members or senators, so that when a member says : I am a member of parliament for so and so, he will be admitted. I have had no trouble nor do I think many members will have trouble. As to the hucksters and beggars, they are to be found in the corridors of this building, and I object to people of this class from Ottawa being allowed such a privilege. I dare say the same thing would apply in every department. I think, however, there is something radically wrong with the heao*

of a department who cannot control the officials or servants under him, and prevent them from allowing these people to come in and take up their time. If I were head of a department I would endeavour to ascertain the business of my clerks and to see that they were kept at work.
It is undignified for a member of parliament to have to carry a pass to any department of the public service ao Ottawa, I shall not do it.

I have certain views with respect to this question and shall say a few words. What I object to is that you should single out any one or two departments of the government of Canada and hedge them around with a sort of divinity which makes them unapproachable. If there are any good reasons for the establishment of these regulations in that department they are good tor every department of the government. The chief ground of my objection is that we are to have hereafter a Naval Department, and I suppose they will hedge themselves around with a sort of divinity, as the Militia Department has done. I consider the regulations objectionable, and I believe that throughout this country they will be so considered. If it is necessary to take steps to prevent hucksters and promoters and men of that class interfering with the work of departments, it seems to me that it would be possible to do that, but the method should be entirely different from the one adopted by the Department of Militia and Defence.
What method do you suggest?

I am not called upon to suggest a method, but if I were invited to do so I think I have initiative enough to do- it. I simply want to voice my protest against the action of the department in this regard because of the singling out of a Militia Department or a Naval Department as being entirely different from any of the other departments of this government. That is my strong objection to the regulation.

As a man of peace, I have been two years a member of this House and have not yet had occasion to call on my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence, I did not however, feel any resentment at what I took to be his courtesy in sending a pass to me ; what I perhaps did resent, in common with a large number of members of both sides of the House, was what appeared to be the injurious suggestion in the letter accompanying the pass that by any possible means a member of parliament could be mistaken for a money-lender. I am not at all sure that the suggestion on the part
of the deputy minister has been recommended by the use of the term referred to by the minister himself. I feel perfectly sure that if the wounded feelings of members were soothed in this respect, the whole matter would blow over with no more ado.

The rule that one pass shall be given to one representative of a newspaper will work awkwardly if the minister insists on these regulations being carried out, in fact it has done so since the regulations were introduced.

This matter was talked over. I understood from my deputy that he intended to communicate with the head office of each newspaper, and ask the newspaper to name its representative in Ottawa, to whom the permanent privilege should be granted. I have no objection to sending half a dozen to one newspaper.

The wording of the latter part of clause 10 is ambiguous and might cause confusion :
Any person desiring admission to the department after these hours must use the west entrance, and upon showing to the policeman satisfactory proof as to his right to enter the building.
After office hours?
After office hours.
I shall bring that to the attention of my deputy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would draw the attention of the government to pages 3, 4 and 5 of volume 1 of the Auditor General's Report. The Auditor General here makes some grave charges that the Senate have been over-paying employees, and also that some members of the House of Commons have not paid for speeches-I do not know whether this overpayment was for printing or for making the speeches. As the Auditor General is the principal safeguard against over-payments, I think that these statements ought to be looked into by the government, and that official should have the assistance of the government in seeing that these over-payments are refunded. I would ask the government if these over-payments have been refunded, and, if not, why not? I see the names of three hon. members of this House who have been over-paid on their indemnities. These names are mentioned and why is it that we have not the names of those servants who have been over-paid and also those members who have not paid for ' their speeches? This information should

be given to the House. I think it is wrong to cover up the name of any one who gets over-payment and fails to make a refund. The over-payments to members are at page N-10. I understand that this has all been refunded. As to these other payments, I understand that the Auditor General has been notifying the proper authorities for some years, but that no action has been taken. I would like to know if these overpayments have been refunded and if not, why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RE OVER-PAYMENTS BY AUDITOR GENERAL.
speechtext: We will look into it.

I notice that the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) is in his place, and therefore, while the matter is fresh in our minds, I would reply to the suggestion which he made that there was an error in the answer which I gave to his question appearing at page 315 of ' Hansard,' The hon. gentleman stated, and no doubt he was under that impression, that there was an error of something like $3,000 in the amount paid for the lighting of the Woods and Canadian buildings for the year ending 31st March, 1909. The hon. gentleman says that the amount I gave is some $3,000 less than appears in the Auditor General's Report. If my hon. friend will turn to the Auditor General's Report for the year ending March 31, 1909, he will find that while the total amount paid for lighting, as shown on that page, is $10,219.62, and while in my statement of the cost of lighting for the year ending March 31, 1909, the amount was given as $7,200 odd, being $3,000 less than that amount, he will find that the amount of $10,219.62 covers the period in respect to the Canadian building from the 20th January, 1908, to the 31st March, 1908, which would be for the preceding fiscal year. He will also find that it includes the lighting of the Queen street building as well, and be will also find that for the lighting of the Woods building there is an amount of $1,836.71 between the 20th January, 1908, and the 26th March,
1908,	which would also be in the previous fiscal year. My hon. friend also will find that it includes the lighting of the Woods building from the 20th January, 1908. So that, between that date and the 31st March, there would also be the lighting which would be for the previous fiscal year. If my hon. friend looks at it carefully he will see that there is no error in the answer that I gave to the House.
Would the hon. minister tell me what volume of the Auditor General's Report he is quoting from?

I am quoting from volume 3 for the fiscal year ended 31st March,
1909.	That.is the fiscal yeaT 1908-9. That Mr. BEST.
is the year to which my hon. friend called attention.
If the minister will look at the Auditor General's Report for that year he will find that for the Woods building alone there is a charge of $3,696.50.
For what year?
1908-9, the one that the minister is looking at. There are two items that must be added together.

That is true; but my hon. friend will observe that that includes the lighting of the Woods building during the shortest winter days from the 20th January, 1908, to the 26th March, 1908, and that ali amounts to $3,696.50.
I am taking the fiscal year 1908-9.
Quite so; the fiscal year ends on the 31st March. That $3,696.50 includes lighting between the 20th January, 1908, and the 26th March, 1908, and that is clearly for the previous fiscal year.

I have the report, which was prepared by an official of the Department of Public Works, showing the different expenditures for 1908-9 and 1909-10. The figures I quoted were prepared by an official of the minister's department.

The hon. gentleman called my attention to the Auditor General's Report for the year 1908-9 and the hdn. gentleman stated to the House that my answer was not in accordance with the Auditor General's Report, but contained an amount $3,000 less. What I want to call the hon. gentleman's attention to is the fact that in the Auditor General's Report the additional $3,000 is shown to be for the lighting of the building during the previous fiscal year and for the Queen street building also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Perley) is right in saying that the question has been only partially answered by one of the departments interested. It ought to include the answers of the other departments. If attention had been called to it I would not have objected to it standing as a notice for an order of the House, because that would be the most convenient procedure.
