Does the deputy Minister of Justice devote himself exclusively to his duties as deputy minister or does he take briefs for private corporations or individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can readily answer the part of the question which refers to the manner in which the deputy Minister of Justice discharges the duties of his official position. That leaves nothing to be desired. I can scarcely find I think, words of praise which would be too high for the manner in which Mr. Newcombe discharges the duties of his position. No one could have the least dissatisfaction with that. In regard to the other question put by the hon. gentleman I have never made inquiry. I have not thought it was any of my affair to do so, I have seen in the newspapers occasionally, very occasionally, his name appearing as arguing a case in the Supreme Court which was not a government case. I think that has occurred in a few instances during perhaps the past two or three years; not more I should say than two or three instances since I have been Minister of Justice. I' can certainly say with assurance, that nothing of that nature has in any degree impaired Mr. Newcombe's usefulness as a public servant or interfered in in any way with the proper discharge of the duties of his office.

I did not question the efficiency of the deputy Minister of Justice in the performance of his duties. I question the propriety of the deputy minister of any department doing business for corporations or indivi-viduals outside his department. I question the propriety of the deputy minister of Justice-occupying that responsible position and receiving the large salary of $7,000 a year, who may possibly be called upon to report or give an opinion on questions between the government and corporations or individuals-acting in a private legal capacity for these corporations or individuals. I think that is a great impropriety and I think it only needs to be mentioned to emphasize its impropriety. I understand that the deputy minister of Justice frequently holds briefs for important corporations and individuals. If the interests pf his private clients digress from the interests of the government surely he cannot serve two masters. A deputy minister should devote his time exclusively to the duties of his office. Now that the matter has been called to the attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of

Justice they should prevail upon the deputy minister of Justice to devote his time exclusively to his official duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not share the view of the hon. gentleman as to the propriety or impropriety of the course which he has been describing. I have of course a very clear recollection of a debate which took place in this House some five years ago when I was Postmaster General, when an attack was made upon me because I was closing the business I had in hand before I became Postmaster General and had appeared in perhaps a dozen or more cases in different courts while I was a member of the government. I maintained upon that occasion my absolute right to take that course; I have not changed my opinion in the least degree. I put this case to the hon. gentleman: If a medical man should happen to be deputy minister of some department and if in case of great emergency he were consulted by some former, or perhaps some new patient, is he not at liberty, supposing it to be at midnight, to relieve suffering and distress, and if he does it and charges a proper fee for it is any body hurt and is there the least impropriety? I can certainly see no impropriety. Now, with regard to a barrister who may be deputy minister of Justice holding a brief in any court for a private client, certainly if his doing so interferes with the discharge of his official duties; if it leads to his work being behind hand, or his time being taken up which properly belongs to the country, then he ought not to do it. But unless that takes place, I can see no reason why the deputy minister of Justice may not be left to his own sense of honour and of the fitness of things, just as any other barrister would be so left. My hon. friend instances I understand, the possibility that interests of some kind whose brief a deputy minister may hold, might perhaps conflict with the public interest. I think I can assure the committee th^t if there were the remotest chance of such a thing the deputy Minister of Justice at any rate, is a man of so delicate a sense of honour that the private brief would instantly be dropped. I have never heard a suggestion that such a thing has ever taken place and I am confident it never has. I am, I repeat, perfectly confident in my own mind that the public interest has never suffered in any degree by the very occasional and rare instances m which Mr. Newcombe has accepted briefs-generally, I think if not always in the Supreme Court-which had been sent to him at the instance of some private litigant.

If the argument of the Minister of Justice is good, then any deputy minister or any official of any department of government can con-Mr. S. SHARPE.
tinue to transact business in competition with other men. That is carrying the principle altogether too far. I have not the honour of knowing the deputy Minister of Justice and no doubt he is a man of a high sense of honour and all that, but he is a human being after all. Now, I understand that this last summer the deputy Minister of Justice went over to the judicial committee of the privy council, left his business here in this country, and held a brief for the Bank of Montreal in an important case in which that bank was interested. Everybody knows that the Bank of Montreal does millions of dollars of business with this country and everybody knows that the Bank of Montreal may possibly have differences with the government which differences would naturally be referred to the Department of Justice for a report. In the first instance that reference would no doubt go to the deputy Minister of Justice because the minister cannot devote his time exclusively to that work, and it is only human nature to favour those who employ us. I say it is a matter of the utmost impropriety for a man occupying the responsible position of deputy Minister of Justice, to hold a brief for the Bank of Montreal which does millions of dollars of business with the government. Notwithstanding the strong language of the Minister of Justice and the fact that he speaks as if he said the last word that is to be said on the subject and as if we should accept his statement gratuitously without any contradiction or question, I submit that it is a matter of the utmost impropriety that the deputy Minister of Justice should hold a brief for the Bank of Montreal, an institution that does millions of dollars of business with the government concerning which grave disputes may arise between that institution and the government of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend's reference to a recent case in connection with the Bank of Montreal gives me an opportunity of saying what I wish to say in regard to it. For some years past, certainly ever since I have been Minister of Justice, Mr. Newcombe has gone each summer to London to look after government cases before the Judicial Committee. That has been done in each instance at my special request. Even if I were able to appear as counsel in a case, I would rather that Mr. Newcombe did it, if it were a matter concerning the British North America Act. I know of no man in this country who in my opinion has a more thorough understanding or a better knowledge of the true spirit and meaning of the British North America Act than Mr. Newcombe has acquired in the years of his practice. Accordingly, it has been at my express desire that he has taken government briefs in matters arising under

the British North America Act when those cases came before the Judicial Committee for consideration. Pursuant to such a request and engaged upon three or four important questions of government litigation, Mr. Newcombe was in London during the month of July and a portion of the month of August last for the sittings of the Judicial Committee, and during that time he was offered this brief for the Bank of Montreal in connection with litigation between that bank and the liquidators of the Ontario bank, which had gone to the Judicial Committee. Now, I cannot see any reason in the world why he should decline that brief. The matter was an important one. If it had not been put into his hands by the Bank of Montreal, it would have been put into the hands of a leading English counsel. It in no way concerned any matter of government business. Mr. Newcombe was not at work in the Judicial Committee when that case was under argument. Even if he had declined the brief, he had to remain in London until the last of the government cases was over; and if at such a time, when he would otherwise have been idle, he is offered a piece of work which does not in any way conflict with or touch government interests, what possible objection there can be to his doing it I am not able to see. In this particular instance, I do not think I knew it beforehand; but when we met, he told me about it in conversation as a matter of ordinary interest between lawyers. He succeeded for his clients, they got good service for whatever fee they paid him, and I certainly was not disposed, in fact, I never thought, to ask him any questions about it or to express the slightest disapprobation of what he had done. I cannot see any reason to change my mind about that. It is perfectly true, there are important interests between the Bank of Montreal and the government, as there are between the government and many other institutions. That is no reason for continual hostility, where the special matter is one that does not in any way affect the public interest. the interest of the government or any of its departments. It seems to me, therefore, that the case is one which very well illustrates that no harm is done to anybody by what has taken place.

We do not want to discuss this question at all on personal grounds. I agree with everything the minister has said with reference to the deputy Minister of Justice, his ability and all his sterling qualities. But there is a very great principle involved in this matter, and I am astonished somewhat that the Minister of Justice has not given some attention to that. What is allowable in a man's private business or in a corporation's own business is not allowable in a government's business. The whole principle involved in this case
is as to whether a man can serve two masters. Whatever will hold good for the deputy Minister of Justice will hold good for every deputy minister, for every high officer, for every officer in the service, no matter where he is. I know that the Prime Minister, who has a long experience in governmental matters, both in opposition and in the government, would not subscribe to the doctrine that a minister should not mind at all whether one, two, three or all of the officials in his department were doing outside work, and never should inquire whether they were or not, so long as they attended to their own duties properly. Whatever is allowed to one deputy minister must be allowed to another ; but there is no deputy ministership in the government upon which the duty devolves more to be clear and clean from outside entanglements than that of the Deputy Minister of Justice, because he has something to do with every department in regard to disputes which are constantly arising and which are referred to his department. There is one other point which I wish to bring strongly to the attention of the minister and the House. Just as soon as you allow a deputy minister to take outside work without curb, just so soon you cause dissatisfaction on the part of other deputy ministers, and you destroy the morale and discipline of the service. But there is another thing stronger still. The moment you allow a deputy minister to engage in outside work which brings him money, that very moment you throw him open to suspicion which may be unfounded, but which goes far towards destroying his usefulness. Therefore, it is not fair to a deputy minister himself to allow him to engage in outside work. I see the Prime Minister has gone out, but I doubt very much if he will stand by the doctrine enunciated by the Minister of Justice. If he does, it is a question of so much importance that it certainly deserves the consideration of parliament.

This matter was brought to the attention of the House in the session of 1906. It may be as well to remind hon. members who were not here then, that my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) moved the following resolution :
That it is inexpedient that any member of the government or deputy head of department should act or appear as barrister, counsel or advocate in any action, suit or proceeding, except where the interests of the Crown are involved, in any court presided over by a judge appointed by the government of Canada.
That resolution was discussed and an amendment to it was offered by the then Minister of Justice (Sir Charles Fitzpatrick) as follows :

That, in the opinion of this House, public business should hare the first claim on the time and attention of each and every member of the government and that the permanent officials of the government should give to the performance of the duties of their respective departments their whole time and attention.
That was the opinion then expressed by the then Minister of Justice, now Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. The members supporting the government voted down the resolution of my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and carried the amendment which I have read, according to which the government were of the opinion that the whole time of every deputy minister should be devoted to the business of his department. If that be still the opinion of the government, no doubt the statement of my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) is quite correct :

No doubt the proceeding in question is a little off colour, but those who know the history of this government will not be surprised because this is not the first, nor the second, nor the third time that similar conduct has been drawn to the attention of the House. I remember distinctly a case some years ago in which an official of the government, a legal gentleman who was receiving a salary of some four ox five or six thousand dollars a year and his expenses, as legal adviser to the government officials in the Yukon, received fees for defending a party who was prosecuted by the government. One of the officials whom this legal gentleman, employed by the government, was obliged by his appointment to advise in the carrying out of his duties, was the collector of customs. The collector of customs had seized a vessel which came into the harbour in violation of the custom law. The captain of the vessel seized did not know to whom he should go for advice and he was advised by another government official, to go to this lawyer who had been retained for the purpose of advising the collector of customs and other government officials in that country. The ship master went to him and was advised by him. The vessel was seized by the Minister of Customs, advised by the same legal gentleman, and the captain of the seized vessel was also advised by him what he should do to get rid of his trouble. Finally the matter was settled, and this gentleman, besides drawing his salary from the government, drew a $700 fee from the captain of the vessel for the advice he gave. In the case we are now discussing, there is not quite so much impropriety, because the deputy Minister of Justice only got a fee for attending to one side of the case, whereas in the other a government official attended to both sides of the case and each side paid him a fee.
Department of Justice-contingencies, $11,000.
Have there been any new appointments or are these simply increases to the old officers provided by law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no increase in the number of clerks. There were some positions vacant twelve months ago which have since been filled.
Who are those?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An appointment, not yet of permanent character, has been made to the position vacted by the death of Mr. Fraser. The appointment to which I am alluding is that of a young man named Edwards, a barrister of the Ontario bar. He is -not doing the work that Mr. Fraser did or receiving the salary. Mr. Fraser's work has been distributed among the other officers of the department. It is now being done by Mr. Power, Mr. Gisborne, Mr. Chisholm and Mr. Pownall, and the work which Mr. Edwards is doing is of a less important character. Then Mr. Leblanc, an advocate from the province of Quebec, has been appointed within the last few months. He is engaged in the general work of litigation instituted against the government with special reference to actions which come under the law of the province of Quebec. These are the only new appointments except that of a stenographer at $500 a year. In the Supreme Court there have been no additions or appointments during the last twelve months, but in the Exchequer Court an appointment has been made of a gentleman whose name at the moment I do not recollect, as clerk in the first division, subdivision ' B '. His work would principally be that of short-hand reporting in the court. He will also act as clerk in the office of the registrar.
In the other two cases, in what division and at what salaries were the appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The salary in respect of the position made vacant by Mr. Fraser has been voted each year at $2,S00, but Mr. Edwards has been appointed at $2,100, and is only receiving that amount at the present time. Mr. Leblanc started as clerk in the second division, subdivision ' A ', at the minimum salary of $1,600. Provision is made in this vote so that if, on April 1 next, he should be considered eligible to receive an increase of $50 there will be means of paying it to him from the appropriation voted.
Department of Militia and Defence-salaries, $137,100.
Will the minister please explain the increase of $8,150 in this vote?

Provision is made in this vote for six new appointments rendered necessary by the fact that the Militia Department has taken over from the Public Works Department the work of constructing the smaller military buildings, that is, those costing up to $15,000 each, and including a lump sum voted of $100,000.
Is not that a duplication of the work of the Public Works Department?
To some extent it will be, but I think it will pay, because I think the Militia Department will be able to do better work and

Hear, hear.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN-more in accordance with their own requirements- it is from that point of view I speak. The department knows better, or ought to know better what it needs, and probably will be able to do with less expensive buildings.
Are there not engineers in all departments

We have engineers. But I was about to point out that we shall require one architect for this new branch at $2,100, two draughtsmen at $1,200 each, and three clerks at $500 each, a total expenditure of $6,000. Then, there are ten promotions involving an increase of $3,950. On the other hand, there have been three resignations, the salaries of those who resigned amounting to $2,800. This leaves a net increase, as shown here, of $8,150.

The Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) was in his seat a few moments ago when the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) raised a question as to the propriety of the deputy Minister of Justice receiving a fee for services from a corporation that does business with the government. I have the greatest respect for the opinion of the Minister of Justice in matters of law and legal interpretation, but, as to the question of propriety in this case, I must beg respectfully to dissent from his view. But, if it be proper for the deputy Minister of J ustice to take a fee from one doing business with the government, I suppose it would be equally proper for the deputy minister of any other department to do the same. I would, therefore, put this question to the Minister of Militia:	We will supposethis is merely a hypothetical question-that the deputy Minister of Militia is approached by the Ross Rifle Company, for instance, and offered $2,000 or $3,000, as the case may be for his services in advising that company with respect to the construction of some peculiar kind of arm, and gives his
services to that concern for two or three weeks; or, suppose he is approached by a manufacturer of clothing who has a contract with the government and is offered and accepts a certain sum of money for his services-would the minister say that that would be a proper act on the part of his deputy minister?

I think my hon. friend need scarcely put a question of that kind because everybody knows it -would be highly improper. But I do not think that his supposititious case is at all on all fours with the one which has been discussed. Because, in the case of my deputy, for instance, in the first place, he is not one who would be qualified to give advice to the Ross Rifle company.

If I may be pardoned- let us assume that he gives value, that he is qualified to render services to the Ross Rifle company. Then, wherein could his case be differentiated from the case of the deputy Minister of Justice?
Assuming that, I say it would be improper.
Then, wherein does that case differ from that of the deputy Minis-of Justice, who has taken a fee from the Bank of Montreal which also has a contract with the government?
It is entirely different, I think.
In what way?

The deputy Minister of Militia, I understand, is a medical man. There are dealers in medical supplies that sell large quantities of medical stores to the government. Suppose that one of these dealers had a lawsuit with another party, would the Minister of Militia consider it proper for his deputy to be called in" to give expert assistance at a large fee to that concern? That is a case on exactly the same footing with the other.
I can only assure my hon. friend that nothing of that kind is being done.

One other question. I would like to ask the Minister of Militia if he expects his deputy minister to give his whole services to the government, or whether it would be competent for his deputy to sell his services to a private individual who had not business with the government.
I certainly believe that my deputy minister does give his whole services-outside of his necessary vacation-to the government.

The hon. minister has not quite answerd my question:	Does he
expect his deputy minister to give his whole time to the service of the government?
I do.
He does not give medical advice to contractors, does he?
I have not heard of it.

The minister has told us that the increase of salaries is due to the fact that a change has heen made in regard to the construction of certain military buildings-those costing not more than $15,000-and that this will come in future, under the direction of this division of the Militia Department; and he tells us that in consequence of that change, this increase in the salary vote is needed.

Part of it,
yes.

The Minister of Militia has shown that he believes that his department can construct buildings required for militia purposes cheaper than the Department of Public Works has done. I hope, for the sake of the country, that they will not cost any more, for under the supervision of the Department of Public Works military buildings, armouries, &c., have cost all the way from 40 per cent to 75 per cent moTe than the estimates. I fail to see why, if the Militia Department is to have the construction of buildings to cost $15,000, it should not have the supervision of the construction of buildings costing from $20,000 to $40,000. Are we to understand that the ability of the Minister of Militia is limited to constructing buildings of $15,000, and that when we come to the construction of a building to cost, according to the estimate, say, $100,000 (and in practice, under the Minister of Public Works $300,000 to $400,000) a brain of the magnitude of that of the Minister of Public Works is required?
Hear, hear.

I am satisfied that the supervision of the erection of these buildings by new officers could not be any worse than it has been in the past under the Department of Public Works. We have evidence from the Atlantic to the Pacific of the utter incapacity of the Public Works Department to handle woTk of this kind properly and in the interests of the country; therefore, even if we have to pay a few dollars more in salaries, or to appoint a few more officers for this purpose, I think it is a move in the right direction, and I only regret that the matteT could not be spread over a larger field and that the Department Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
of Militia could not have under its control the construction of all those buildings, about which, it seems to me, the Minister of Militia should know more, and I believe does know infinitely more than the Minister of Public Works. If you examined the militia I believe you would find that to-day you have nearly as many officers as men in it and a few more officers would not make much difference. My only regret is that the Minister of Militia is not to go a little farther and take over buildings the construction of which cost more than $15,000. The existing system seems to me utterly illogical. The Department of Militia considers that a building of a certain size is required for a certain place and the minister asks for a building to cost $20,000 or $25,000; the Minister of Public Works comes along and puts up a building costing $200,000 or $300,000. That sort of thing has been going on until the people are sick and tired of it, and we have an expenditure of between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 on Militia and Defence. This would not be so bad if it were properly expended, but in many cases throughout this country, under the system now in vogue, buildings have been erected so much larger than the circumstances required that money has thereby been diverted from the proper channels where it would do most good.

I wish to endorse the remarks of my hon. friend. I understand an armoury has been built in Hamilton recently and that the architectural work has been placed in charge of the local militia there; that is to say, that the Department of Public Works did not originate the plans. That armoury is endorsed by every person who knows anything about armouries as being possibly the best laid out and the best in Canada. I am very pleased to see the Minister of War take chaTge of this work to some extent, because I feel that we ought to have our public works carried out in the same way as they are in the United States. In the United States and also in England and other countries the inspection of all public work of any character is carried on by the Engineering Department of the War Department. Young and old engineers have charge of all work and no contractor can get away with bad work when these inspectors are on the job. Possibly in only three instances in the history of the engineering corps in the United States has there been any complaint, or any default by the officers in charge. The result is that the government gets a dollar's worth for its dollar, and when a contractor takes a contract for a public work he knows that the inspector of that work is from the engineering staff, a fully competent man, and that he will have to carry on that- work strictly according to his contract. I hope that this gov-

eminent will see its way clear to expand that principle. Every one knows that we are each year passing many very competent. young men through the Military College at Kingston. They graduate into other lines of life after they leave the college, they are engineers, and they go into civil life. We do not seem to be able to tlnd places for these graduates, many of them brilliant men, in the Canadian service, but if there was an engineering staff in connection with the militia, and if all the work carried on by the Canadian government was placed in charge of these men, who would look forward to a life service and a pension at the end of it, this House would feel satisfied that the work would be carried on properly and that good value would be secured for the country. In addition to that, the Royal Military College would be then fulfilling its functions and would be giving value to this country for the money expended on it. I heartily endorse the proposal, I am only sorry that the value of the buildings is not increased from, say, $15,000 to $40,000 or $50,000, which would take in all military buildings.

The arbitrary amount of $15,000 has been fixed subject, of course, to adjustment afterwards, if found necessary. The idea was that the smaller buildings costing $15,000 and less could be constructed with less trouble and more rapidly by the Militia Department than by the Public Works Department for this reason: When the Public Works Department constructs a military building it must, of course, look to the Department of Militia for its plans. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend, the case of the Hamilton Drill Hall, which he rightly says is, perhaps, the finest in the whole Dominion of Canada, perhaps of its kind anywhere, the building was constructed by the Public Works Department, but perhaps special deference was paid in this particular case to the views of the local militia officers.
Was it designed by a Public Works engineer?
Oh, yes, entirely so, but based upon recommendations made through my department.
As is always the case.

Difficulties are constantly cropping up. Something is discovered in the course of construction, some change that ought to be made, we are not there to look after it and an error very likely is made. There is this to be said, and my hon friend, I think, will not object to my saying it: The Department of Public Works is desirous of constructing handsome and highly creditable public buildings and is a little too prone pos-33
sibly to expend a larger sum of money than would be absolutely necessary for the, requirements of the militia department, particularly in the smaller places. We want a larger number of armouries. We need hundreds and we cannot get them unless we bring the cost down to a reasonable figure. We are going to make an effort-we may fail, but we will do our best to succeed-to construct armouries for a small number of men within a reasonable expenditure. The larger buildings will be left in the hands of the Public Works Department. This will be desirable with all the machinery they possess.. Expenditures for large armouries, costing a quarter of a million or more, and large barracks, such as are to be constructed in Toronto and Montreal, will remain under the control of the Department of Public Works. My hon. friend has referred to the system in the United States of placing all this work under the control of engineers. That is quite true and that is what is proposed to be done now. I did not mention that we have considerable part of the staff that will enable us' to do the work economically. My hon. friend referred to the desirability of affording employment for graduates of the _ Royal Military College. He will be glad ' to know that we are doing more and more of that. We are particularly in the civil branches and in the military branch of the service, employing nearly 100 to-day, while fifteen years ago we only had two.
Not all permanent?
No, but most of them.

The move made by the hon. Minister of Militia is certainly along the right line. At almost every district headquarters there is now, and if there is not there should be, a district engineer. That officer with a staff of a very few men could almost revolutionize the military buildings in each locality. For instance, take Kingston; there are, as every one knows who has visited the Royal Military College, dozens of jobs to be done but if you have to go through the regular routine of calling for tenders it will take a great deal of time and cost a tremendous amount of money. I need only cite the cottages that have been referred to on other occasions by my hon. friend from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) as an instance of the absolute waste of money in this regard. With the engineer in charge and a few men at his disposal there is not a district headquarters or camp that could not have' permanent buildings at a nominal cost, such as would be of absolute advantage to the country. Every year the stores are hauled out from some building where



they are kept to camp at some loss from wear and tear and in other regards. They are not properly cared for because they cannot be properly cared for in tents, and therefore^ I maintain that in all these localities the engineers could very properly-be employed at this work of building drill -iheds and small armouries. The engineer* and one or two of his permanent officials' could do this work where there is no contract, or extras, or rake-off, for half of what it would cost to erect such buildings under the ordinary conditions. I very highly commend the move of the minister

I have only one remark to add and it will come home more especially to members on this side of the House, as to the quality of the work done by the Public Works Department. All we have to do is to go into this new wing to the west of us. Whoever laid out that wing followed the architecture of the rest of the building, but forgot, in the glad moments of picturing out his beautiful design, that there would have to be such things as heating and ventilation. The result is, that no arrangement was made for wiring, heating and ventilating the building, until it was completed, and now upon going into the rooms you see the same old method of piping as that which appears in the rest of the building which was erected long before they had such thing as steam heating. It reminds me very much of the story of a Chinaman who was employed to make a man a pair of trousers. The trousers happened to have a patch on them when finished. The man had sent the Chinaman a pattern and he had made use of it in this way. The Chinaman then made a new pair of trousers and when they were completed the customer found that the patch had been taken from the old ones and put on the new ones too. So, in this new building the heating pipes, instead of being hidden away in the wall, as they would be under modern conditions, are exposed just the same as they are in old buildings, so that the harmony of the buildings is preserved in that respect. Anybody who has the slightest idea of a modern building, going into the rooms of this new wing, will be shocked to find how the Public Works engineering staff does its work.

I certainly do sincerely trust that the result of this change will be that we shall get these small armouries built at a less cost than heretofore. May I express the hope that my gallant and brave friend from Victoria and Haliburton, (Mr. Hughes), will be able, a year or two from now, to congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden), upon the very great economies that have been effected in connection with the construction of these Mr. HUGHES.
buildings. I may say that my desire, and the desire of all the members of the government, is to erect these buildings as economically as we can. I was very glad indeed when my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence, stated that with the staff which they had in connection with the Department of Militia and perhaps with some slight increase, they -would be able to take charge of these smaller armouries. If the experiment proves the success which I trust it will be, it will afford us very great pleasure to carry it to a still further degree. We have a great deal of work in the Department of Public Works. We are not able to keep pace with the demand from the various sections of the country, for ordinary buildings, such as post offices and custom houses. The country is growing so rapidly, that the chief architect, with his present staff, has not been able to get along with the work as rapidly as I would like him to do. Just a word with regard to my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), who knows-I would not say a good deal-but a little about everything, and who thinks he knows perhaps more about architecture than the regular experts of the architectural branch of the Department of Public Works. The hon. gentleman complains about this western wing. I think he is not doing his knowledge of architecture justice, when he makes that complaint. People who know what good buildings are, have spoken in the highest terms of this western wing.
Would the minister point out why there is no provision made in one single room for ventilation?

The hon. gentleman for North Simcoe complains of the fact that the heating apparatus is in the room .beside the walls, instead of being concealed. There are many people who prefer that kind of heating arrangement.

The minister is entirely mistaken. I did not object to the architectural design. I said that the architecture wras very good. What . I objected to, was that the pipes which convey the heat throughout the building were all stuck on the walls with nails and hooks.
I presume the hon. gentleman means that the radiators should be placed inside the walls.
If the minister does not know the difference between a radiator and a steam pipe we will let him have his own way.

Many people prefer the present mode of heating the western wing, and I do not object to the architect adopting that system. I do not think that any competent and fair minded judge will say

that the western wing is not well constructed and is not creditable to the department.

We welcome the criticism by the Minister of Militia on the extravagant policy pursued by the Minister of Public Works in the past. Will the Minister of Militia in his new sphere as builder and contractor employ clerks of works who are not builders or contractors or even mechanics, as the Minister of Public Works used to do?
I hope the hon. gentleman will not take that as admitted because I do not contradict it.
We had a case where men were employed by the Public Works Department as clerks of works, and these men were tailors.
That is just a single case, ten years ago.
Will the Minister of Militia employ for this duty artisans of experience or will he continue the system of engaging politicians?
In addition to the permanent employees it may be necessary to employ some outside men from time to time.
Will they be experienced men?
That is my intention.
Will these men have to be recommended by a supporter of the government?
I would be disposed to have an officer of my department visit a particular work and report what would be necessary in the employment of extra men.
Will the increased staff of the Militia Department, necessary to take charge of these buildings, result in a corresponding decrease in the staff of the Public Works Department?
The demands for public buildings are so increasing that we will have to increase the staff rather than diminish it.
At what date will the Militia Department take over the construction of the public buildings which are to be placed under its control?
Very likely at the beginning of the fiscal year, in April.

Will the minister have sufficient staff to undertake the construe-tion of such works as have already been determined upon, or will this change be ever used as an excuse for delay.
33}
Never.
Will the Minister of Militia have sufficient staff to proceed at once with the construction of such works as have months before this been determined upon?
That is my expectation.
In some instances heretofore the government have asked the municipalities to provide sites and in other instances the government purchased the sites. What will be the policy as to that in the future?

In some instances a municipality in order to induce the government to erect a building on certain lands which it owned was not only willing but anxious to give the site. Where the municipality desires to contribute the site the department will be glad to accept it. In other cases where it is absolutely necessary to have a militia building, if the local authorities do not feel disposed to give a site my department will purchase a site as has been done in the past by the Department of Public Works.
When a municipality presents a site to the department is there not a concession given to the municipality in the way of allowing them to use the drill shed on certain public occasions.

Yes, there are cases where an agricultural society may own property or where the municipality may hold the property for such a society, and in these cases an arrangement is made. In one case I have in mind the department pays rental on a certain portion of the building constructed on these grounds for military purposes, and that is an advantage to the municipality and to the department. We shall be glad to do this in other cases when the occasion arises.
How are these sites to be selected?
By the municipal authorities, or the local military authorities, with the assistance of representatives from the engineering branch of my department, or by all three.
Not by the Reform Association?
No.

Then the Minister of Militia will have a new policy, because last session I read an advertisement from a western Ontario newspaper calling the Reform Association of the municipality to select the site for a public building.
For the Militia Department?
No, the Public Works Department.
It would be to advise as to the site.
The Reform Association put an advertisement in the newspaper calling the friends together for the purpose of selecting a site for a public building. Will the Minister of Militia continue that policy?
You would hardly call that a policy, that would be a very impolitic thing to do.
Will the Minister of Militia answer?

I shall look for the best information we can get. I have already named three sources of information, and I may add that I would not object to advice from the Reform Association or even from the Conservative Association. I would not object to good advice from any source. Our object is to locate our building in the best situation, and the Reform Association might have correct views about that, and equally so the Conservative Association.
What about the middleman?
I have not had any experience of that kind.

I would like to ask the Minister of Militia and Defence one question. His department is to have buildings not to cost more than $15,000. Suppose the Minister of Public Works, in the future as in the past, should consider that a certain place ought to have an armoury to cost $20,000, how would you decide that matter? Would you call out the militia to settle it?
No, I think I would decide that.

The hon. minister has not been able to decide it in the past, according to his own statement. He has frequently said that a building of a certain size was suitable to a certain place, and the Minister of Public Works has put up a much more expensive one to the detriment of the militia, because it has prevented people in other parts of the country getting buildings that would serve the purpose. I can fancy the Minister of Public Works trying to get control, so as to put up buildings costing $20,000 or more, in order to spend the money himself. Therefore I do not know how you are going to settle the matter.

What is the policy of the government with regard to the mainten-Mr. BLAIN.
ance of drill sheds in small villages? I understood that some years ago the government decided to store the arms of each battalion at headquarters and to do away with these small buildings, but I find that some of them are going up again.

Some years ago, when the Lee-Enfield rifle was first introduced here, there seemed to be an idea that it must be so carefully handled that all the rifles should be kept under a caretaker at a central point. It was found by experience that that was not necessary, and now the policy is that when the headquarters of a regiment composed of eight companies accommodates sufficiently all the companies of that regiment, we should have onlv one armoury at a central point; but when the companies are situated a long way apart, ten or fifteen or twenty miles, then there should be either an armoury for each of the companies, or one for such companies as are situated more closely together. That is the policy at present, to have a much larger number of small armouries throughout the country.

Before this item passes, I would like to remind the minister that last session I brought to his attention the necessity of establishing an armoury or a drill shed in the town of Pembroke, and. in view of what he has just said, I think that would be wise. We have only one company in the town, and the nearest other company is at the town of Renfrew, about thirty miles distant.

I should think that would be a very proper point at which to have a small armoury.

There are increases as follow :	None in First Division, Subdivision A ; Subdivision B, an increase of one ; Second Division, Subdivision A, an

increase of two ; Second Division, Subdivision B, an increase of three ; Third Division, Subdivision A, an increase of three ; Third Division. Subdivision B, an increase of six, making a total of fourteen.	'	.
These increases were urged 'by the chief officers of the department as being absolutely necessary. There are some few_ increases in salaries. In the First Division, Subdivision A, there are eight statutory increases of $100 each. Then authority was given under sec. 38 chap. 15 to add $200 to the minimum salary of the First Division, Subdivision A, to be paid the assistant engineer, making his salary $3,000. First Division, Subdivision B, fifteen increases at $100 each and one at $50. There is a new appointment at $2,100.
What is the explanation of the new appointment?
The official is required according to the report made by the deputy minister.
Has the appointment been made?
There has been an appointment made and a promotion from the Second Division, Subdivision A.
What auoui the fourteen new appointments?
These are all in the Third Division.
Did they pass the civil service examination?
They must before the appointments are made. We are making provision for the increase.
Among those who have already passed the examination, could not men be found to fill these positions?

When we get a vote, we give notice that a certain number of clerks are required and they are appointed on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission after competitive examinations have taken place. The commissioners can recommend from among those who have already passed if there are any available. In fact the commissioners make the appointments. In the case of promotions, they are made on the recommendation of the deputy head, but there must be also a certificate from the _ Civil Service Commission as to qualification.
Does the department require that the deputy minister shall give his whole service to the government?
That question has never arisen because he does give his whole time to it.
Does the minister believe he could give a sufficient service if he were permitted to devote part of his time to outside interests?
I would not think so. His duties are of such a nature that he could not.
Why should a different rule apply to the Public Works Department to that which applies to the Justice Department?

I would say that the position of a lawyer is different from that of almost anybody else in the community. A lawyer becomes more efficient and more able to discharge his duties by the greater practice that he has. I should think that, if the deputy minister should undertake to argue a case now and then which would bring him into touch with the best legal minds of the country, and could do it without neglecting his official duties, it would be an advantage to him and to the public service.

But that is entirely contrary to the policy of the government as set forth in the resolution which I read just before six o'clock.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I was giving my opinion. I was not asked what the rule was.

I pointed out that this government had favoured a resolution which was adopted by this House declaring that in future the deputy ministers were to give their whole time to the public service. But now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) opens the door to any by saying that this may apply to some, ,but not to others. What has taken place to cause the government to change its policy, and what order in council has been passed on the subject?

I was asked my opinion as to whether there might be a distinction as between the position of the deputy Minister of Justice and that of another deputy. I stated my opinion entirely apart from the resolution. I am not aware whether the deputy Minister of Justice has devoted his time to other business or not; and it would not be my place to answer as to that. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) was here when the items of the Justice Department were under consideration, and I presume he gave the committee such information as was desired.

The minister bases his distinction on the fact that the deputy Minister of Justice is a lawyer, and so improves by carrying on practice. Does he wish to state that his own deputy minister does not improve? I do not catch the distinction the hon. gentleman makes.
There is a great distinction; my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) knows it.
I have not had it explained yet.

The Minister of Public Works has clearly stated that the whole time of the deputy Minister of Public, Works must be devoted to the duties of his office, and that one in that position could not give good service if he was allowed to devote part of his time to private practice. But when asked about the case of the deputy Minister of Justice, he explains that in the case of lawyers it is different- Would he change his answer with regard to the deputy Minister of Public Works if that gentleman happened to be a lawyer?
I do not know that I would. A lawyer would not be so well qualified, speaking generally, to discharge the duties of a department like the Public Works, as would a reliable business man.
But that does not apply to the minister?
The minister is an exception to all rules in the opinion of my honourable friend.

Will the minister please explain what necessity there is for an increase of fourteen clerks in his department in one year? That seems a very large increase, especially in view of the fact that the Public Works Department is handing over a portion of its business to the Department of Militia and Defence. The increase of work must be verv rapid to require an incease of fourteen this year, and, presumably, an equal number next year.

I do not know what will be necessary next year, but this increase is certainly necessary this year. Several of the new appointments are to be in the architectural branch. The chief architect has asked very urgently for an increase in his staff. He has not been able to keep up with his work. There are a number of buildings that I would like to have seen erected in pursuance of the votes parliament has made, but it has been quite impossible to keep up with the work of preparing plans. And that is an index of what exists in the different branches of the service. The business of the country is growing very rapidly, and, as cities and towns increase in number and importance, there is necessarily a growing demand for public accommodation in the way of post offices, custom houses and other buildings, the construction of which adds greatly to the work of the architectural branch, and, of course, to the need of clerical force required to keep pace with the work. The hon. gentle-Mr. HEIGHTEN.
man (Mr. Sproule) knows as well as I do how the country is growing, especially in the west, and realizes that this must increase the work of the department.

It does seem to me that a staff of 257 ought to be a fairly large one for a single department. That was the number last year, and this year it is increased to 271. That would undoubtedly indicate a greatly increased amount of work thrown on the department. Yet, on looking over the estimates, as compared with the previous year, I do not see that there is very much more work. It would almost seem that, year by year, these people do less work and require more hands to do it. From a business standpoint, one would think that this staff would be capable of handling a great deal of work in the way of preparing plans and specifications, making estimates and drawing contracts. I do not know what the increase was last year over the year before, but if there was a proportionate increase, tho staff is certainly growing very fast.
I am glad my hon. friend realizes that there is no unusual increase in the appropriation. I would agree with him that there is not, except as is required by the increased demands of the country.	-
How about outside architects?

But the disbursements amount to a good many millions of dollars. And I must say there is one very important work of the department, the dredging, on which we are trying to keep much closer watch than in the past. We have one engineer who is devoting his special attention to that work. We try to keep track of the different dredges in all sections of the country, to keep track of the inspectors and to watch closely the reports on the work. That requires the attention not only of one engineer, but also of assistants. With regard to the services of outside architects, we have endeavoured to keep the work within the department as closely as possible, but I am sorry to say we have not been able to do so entirely.
Does the minister expect to do it in the future with the new staff?

That will depend on how the work increases. We have not the accommodation we would like, but if we had the accommodation I think it would be better to engage even a larger staff, so that we might do the work as much as possible within the department. I have in mind three or four buildings for the coming year, the plans of which will be prepared by outside architects.
What buildings are they?
One at Rigaud and two in Montreal. I cannot at the moment think of others.

The minister says he requires more assistance in the architectural branch. One would .suppose that men of that class would be among the better paid officials. I do not see how you could get good architects' for the salaries mentioned here. For instance, in Division 3-B, there are salaries of $800, $775, $550 and $500. Yet I notice that the chief increases asked for by the minister are in the two lower grades, Subdivisions A and B of the Third Division. There are nine inereases in this division, more than one half of the total number. This hardly agrees with the minister's statement that he was short of architects; I would suppose that the architects would be a better class of men with higher salaries.

My hon. friend will notice one increase in Subdivision B of the First Division and two in Subdivision A of the second and two in Subdivision B of the second. These will all provide for architects of greater experience and then there are two in Subdivision A of the Third Division. My hon. friend is aware that a good deal of work in the department would be in the way of draughting, acting under the instructions of more experienced men. Young men are taken into the department and as they gain experience, if they discharge their duties efficiently are promoted into the higher divisions, but in the lower divisions they are doing exceedingly useful work for a few years.

You had in that branch, last year in the main estimates 257. That was raised to 243, but in the Supplementary Estimates, you provided for one clerk in the First Division, three in the second, four in 2-B and three in 3-A, one in 3-B and two messengers. That was an increase of 20 last year, and now we are asked foi an increase of 14 more this year.
Was that 20 above the 257?
Yes.
There must have been a number of vacancies because we are only asking now for 271 altogether.

I suppose there can be a vacancy if a friend needs the position. I take it for granted that there will probably be in the supplementary estimates this year some additional ones. There are different places where they can be loaded on the country and they are being loaded on in my judgment at a very rapid rate. This same increase in staff has gone on for several years past, and the increase in
numbers seems to be out of proportion to the increased work to be done. I cannot understand it, it is unnecessary and the only explanation I can find is that from year to year there is less work being done individually by the clerks through shorter hours, and one thing and another. I have often been amused and sometimes annoyed at the way civil servants carry on their work. We come here as members of parliament and our time is usually much occupied if' we endeavour to keep up with the work of the House. You have business to do with a department, but you cannot find the clerks you want before 10 o'clock; they are supposed to be there at 9.30 but there are always certain officials not there and you cannot be attended to.
Would my hon. friend give an instance in my department?

I have not had very much to do with the minister's department for the past two years, but I had sometimes before that, and I am quite satisfied from what I know of the customs of the employees and their hours of labour there, that it would be found just the same in the Public Works Department as in the ojher departments. Then we go to the committee work at 11 o'clock and are obliged to work until nearly one o'clock. We go to a department to get something done but that is impossible because so many officials have gone to lunch. You may not find them at their offices before 2 o'clock or 2.30. Then, members have to be at the House at 3 o'clock, they are anxious to be here at least until routine business is disposed of, and it is four o'clock before it is possible to again go to the departments and then you find that some of the officials have left their offices. It seems to me that in many of these departments the hours of labour must be very very short. In a private business such conditions would not be tolerated.
I suggested a few years ago, and a number of times since, that all these officials should be given a certain definite lunch hour and that during that time the departments should be closed. That would be better and more convenient for the members of parliament. It would economize the members' time and prevent many useless trips to the department. A few years ago the civil servants were supposed to work from 9.30 o'clock until 4, now I understand it is from 9.30 to 5 oclock, but if you go to their offices you will find many of them out before that time. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the civil servants as a whole are not hard working people, many of them are hard working men and women, in fact many are overworked, and they do remarkably well considering the chance they have to do their work. Their

time must be broken into from hour to hour a great deal and therefore they cannot do as much work as one could who sat there' quietly on from hour to hour and was not disturbed. I think that there is a large proportion that does mighty little work and puts in very short hours. I would suggest-and I suggest it again because of my experience from year to year and the difficulty of doing any work in the_ departments-the advisability of allowing them a given time at noon, let it be known, and then members of parliament will not be frittering away their time running down to these departments every hour hoping to find these clerks in with the idea of doing some business with them As it is now, and it has been for many years, it is a great source of annoyance and a great waste of time to members of this House and it is very little satisfaction to them in their endeavour to do any work with the departments here during the session.

This is the first intimation I have had that any member of parliament has been inconvenienced in getting access to any of the officers of the department, or in seeing any of the clerks. I certainly have never had a complaint, and I have never heard of any complaint being made to any other minister.
If the minister had been in this House he must have heard this complaint before.

If the hon. gentleman desires any information in the department, he ought to call upon the minister or the deputy minister, who would ring for the clerk, whose presence was desired, and if he was so late in getting to the office as the hour which my hon. friend speaks of, he certainly would be reprimanded, and I do not think it would be likely to occur again. I think it would be only fair, if the hon. gentleman has any complaint, to make it to the minister or to the deputy and the particular clerk in fault, would be reprimanded. As I have said, I have heard no complaint at all, and I am sure that the heads of the departments would be quite ready to take any steps which might be necessary with regard to any clerk who was at fault in the way that my hon. friend speaks of. Just a word to my hon. friend with regard to the numbers. My hon. friend stated that we had in the supplementary estimates provided for 14 additional clerkships.
In the main estimates for six.
Quite so.
And in the supplementary estimates for 14, I think it was.
Yes, in the supplementary estimates. I would inform my hon. friend that this was for the purpose of making promotion. We had to take these additional votes before the promotions could take place.
How can it be promotions, when it is in the supplementaries?
We provided for a clerkship in the 1st Division of Subdivision B.
Yes.

And by getting that vote we could take a clerk from the lower division and promote him into the higher division, but it would leave the lower clerkship vacant. That is the way it was done because we are only asking for 271 this year altogether.
And you had how many before?
257. The supplementaries did not mean any increase in the number. It was merely putting clerks in a higher division.
You had last year 257 clerks and this year the number is raised to 271. Are these not individual entities that make up that number?
Yes.
Can you increase a number and still have the same number of clerks?

No, it means an increase in the positions, an increase in numbers. But, the hon. gentleman stated that in our main estimates last year we had an increase and he made the number 257. Then my hon. friend thought that we had 14 in the supplementaries. If we had done that last year, that would have made 271. If we added 14 more this year, that would be 285, instead of 271. We are not making any increase.
I think my hon. friend's calculation is wrong. How many had you in the main estimates last year?
I was taking my hon. friend's own figures. My hon. friend said we had an increase of 14, and he said that we had 243 in the main estimates.
Then how many were added?
In the main estimates?
My hon. friend said it was 14. In the main estimates last year we asked for 243.
How do you get it up to the 257, which you show in your estimates now?
In the supplementaries there were 14. Add 14 to 243 and that makes 257. Now we are adding 14 this year.
Who was right and who was wrong? I said you added fourteen last year, the minister denied it and said that this was only a change of place. Now you add fourteen more this year.
I think we misunderstood each other. I understood my hon. friend to say that wre had 257 in the main estimates last year and that we had then added fourteen to the number in the supplementaries.
No.
And that now we add fourteen more. But I see that what my hon. friend meant was-and no doubt I misunderstood him-that the number was 243 in the main estimates. I have no doubt it was my fault.

I have not looked back further than the estimates of last year. I assume that in the supplementaries this year, as in those of last year, there will be an additional number provided for. There were fourteen in the supplementary estimates last year and there may be more in the supplementaries this year.
I do not think there will be any in the supplementaries this year. I have no intimation that there will be.

It may be so and it may not. But the rate at which they are going seems a very rapid one and out of all pro.-portion to the needs of the country. I cannot understand why the minister needs to add fourteen or fifteen in the civil service branch of one department every year and this going on from year to year. I do not think that the work is there to be done, there must be some other explanation of it.
No, that is the explanation; the officials of the department claim that they require further assistance.

I fail to understand why the minister needs an increase of thirty-four employees in the department in the last two years, especially as the amount of public work that has been constructed in the Dominion in the last two years, I suppose, has not been as great as it was four years before. When hon. gentlemen opposite returned from the general election in 1908, and when the House met in January the appropriations for public works throughout the Dominion were cut down by millions of dollars. Yet, notwithstanding that, in that year the minister engages twenty clerks and comes back to this House and asks for fourteen more, making an increase
of thirty-four employees in the department or over ten per cent, and on that basis we will have the right to expect that there will be more clerks provided for in the supplementary estimates of the present year. I think I would be safe in saying that the increase in two years would be forty clerks in the department. The minister has not given us any reasonable explanation of why he requires forty more clerks in the last two years when the amount of public works constructed is not equal to the amount in the two years prior to that time.

My hon. friend, I think, is in error as to that. He is quite correct in saying that there was quite a considerable reduction in the estimates, but the public works which have been going on have certainly been steadily increasing There may be one year during which there was a decrease, but, taking one year with another, public works throughout the country are steadily increasing and this year the appropriation is very large. If my hon. friend will look at the appropriation on capital account and then take that upon income he will see that it amounts to in the vicinity of $14,000,000. That is a large amount of money, but it is expended on probably 1,000 public works from one end of Canada to the other. We have to have an increased number on the engineering staff and on the overseeing staff and in the architectural branch and the accounting branch. Then the dredging work, both contract and government work, has increased enormously and requires careful watching. By having the requisite staff to attend to that -work a great deal more will be saved to the country than the increased salaries will amount to. I can assure the committee that there is not a single position asked for by me that was not requested by the responsible head of the branch and concurred in by the deputy minister.

I think I am safe in saying that in 1907 and 1908 the appropriation for public works was as great as it was last year, and yet the minister says* he wants forty more employees to do apparently less work. It is the minister who is responsible for the expenditure of the public money and he cannot shift the responsibility by saying that he relies on his subordinates.

For instance, when returns are asked for by the House and not brought down, I am told that the delay is caused because the staff is not sufficient to attend to this work and discharge the other pressing needs of the service. I believe the heads of the branches who have recommended this increase in the staff are trustworthy, and I think we should give them the assistance they require to properly perform their duties.
The expenditure on public works was as great two years ago as it is to-day, and yet the minister says he requires 40 more clerks now.

The hon. gentleman cannot measure the quantity of work done by the total appropriation, because while a large amount may be expended on ten or twelve different public works, not nearly as much assistance would be required as if this money were divided between a great many public works scattered over the Dominion. I venture to say there are more public works under way and in contemplation to-day than ever before in the history of Canada. The rapid development of the three, prairie provinces and British Columbia have caused enormous demands upon us, and we will have to make further provision in the supplementary estimates for pressing public works.

I would not for the world say anything that might cause the minister to diminish the efficiency of his staff, but at the same time it might be well for him to look into the quality of his' officials and not concern himself so much about the quantity. I have in mind one instance which ought to impress the minister with the necessity of securing efficient servants in order that he may not lose the esteem of his own party in the country. Previous to my election two years ago, the Minister of Public Works saw fit, very hurriedly, about the first of October, 1908, to commence a public work in the neighbourhood of my constituency. The officials of the department, assisted by the faithful in the constituency, gathered togther very rapidly all the loose men around the town and hurried them to the trenches on the Assiniboine river, where they were supplied with steady work until the election was over. The public work then undertaken was in some degree completed, but unfortunately the officials of the department did not seem to do their work properly and a certain solicitor of the city of Portage la Prairie, who is a faithful adherent of this government,, had charge of procuring the title of the land on which this public work was located. By the way, there was no immediate necessity for this public work, but in order that it might be done just at the opportune time in relation to the date of the election, it was hurried through before any title to the land was procured or arrangement made.
What was that work?

The cut made in the Assiniboine river, some few miles from Portage la Prairie, in the constituency of Macdonald.
Mr. PUGSLEY
My hon. friend saysl there was no necessity for that work.

I said the immediate necessity for it did not appear at the timel except in connection with the date of the election. The only time it was required was about four years previously, and no flood had occurred since.
You cannot tell when you may have a flood.

This public work was hurried along on the 1st of October, 1898, and as the title to the land had not been secured and the land not paid for, certain of the minister's friends in the town, including the solicitor I have spoken of, had to go down in their own pockets and float a note in the bank to purchase this land for the department. They did this of their own accord it appears. The note fell due and the officials of the department, lagging behind, did not attend to the matter and these poor gentlemen in Portage la Prairie had to pay that note themselves. The solicitor, still faithful in his attachment to the party, pleaded with the department to get down to business and to reimburse them this money which they were good enough to put up in order to hurry forward this public work so as to defeat the Tory candidate in Portage la Prairie. But it was impossible for the solicitor to make any progress because of this very limited staff which the minister is now trying to augment. Time went by and the patience of the solicitor became somewhat exhausted. Finally his party fealty seemed to waiver and he wrote the minister in despair, telling him that before he would have anything more to do with his department he would have an understanding first about it, and he further pointed out that if he had been dealing with the Manitoba government, which is conducted on business lines, he would have had no such trouble because as he stated in this letter the matter would have been attended to in a businesslike way. This solicitor then threatened to charge up against the Public Works Department the interest on the note which the friends had to pay at the bank, as part of the costs of the transfer of the land. I am sure that in the light of experience such as that my good friends around me will cease bantering the minister about increasing the staff of his department. If the minister would only look to it that when he wants to hurry forward public works in preparation for an election he has an efficient staff and does not have to call on the faithful adherents to dip down into their own pockets and buy the right of way in a hurry, there might be some excuse for his present action. I may

say, that this same attorney was finally dealt with by the department and became the Liberal candidate in the last local election. We will not criticise anything that will improve the efficiency of the department, but the point that my hon. friend from North Grey has made is well taken. As we know, the work of the department is measured by the appropriations, and the appropriations were never so great as they were just before the last elections, and we expect will never be so great again until the next election comes along. If the minister can tell us why the staff to-day should be greater than in 1908, when there was a larger appropriation for public works, so far as I am concerned the appropriation may go.

The Minister of Public Works tells us that if a member does not find a clerk in the office that member should go and complain to him. Does he think that a member of parliament is sent here to run around and hunt up ministers. Why, sometimes you will stand outside( their door for hours before you can see them.
Oh, no.
All of them are not that way, but some of them are.
I am sure we would all be very glad to see the hon. gentleman.

If the minister thinks it is the duty of a member of parliament to hunt up a minister to make a complaint to him about an official, he must think he is talking to children. He is supposed to have responsible men at the head of his staff, and it is their duty to see that the work is properly done. The minister says he has never before heard complaints, but I have made the same complaint in this House for some years back, and that complaint has been made time and again by other hon. gentlemen. The statement of the hon. gentleman is somewhat picayune coming from a minister of the Crown.
The hon. gentleman says he has not been in my department for a number of years.

The Minister of Public Works cave as his reason for the employment of additional clerks that he wanted some of them to watch the men who are placed in charge of the dredging. There is no doubt they need watching, but it would be much better for the minister to dismiss some of these fellows who require watching than to nay the men who are needed to watch them.' He told us that there was a lack of efficiency amongst the clerks who look after the dredging.

I made no such statement. I said we had a great amount of
government and contract dredging going on all over the country and that we endeavoured to keep in the closest touch possible with that work.
Since when?
Since a considerable time.
You must have commenced very recently.

Oh, no. We have made that the special duty of one of the engineers of the department who has assistants under him, and we keep in touch with the dredging work all over the country, getting returns regularly, having these [DOT] returns carefully looked into, testing out the work so as to keep up a sort of constant inspection upon the dredging. That does not at all imply that there is any inefficiency on the part of the staff. That is a proper business like precaution which I am sure the House will approve. We are spending several millions of dollars a year on work of this character and it is only a proper discharge of the duty we owe to the country that we should keep in constant touch with the work in order to see that it is being carried out honestly, and in the best interest of the country.

When the Minister of Public Works starts out to give information in reply to any question asked him here he reminds me of the man who was asked to sing ' Annie Laurie ' and he sang ' Highland Mary ', and when he was asked why he sang ' Highland Mary ' and said there was more 'divarsion' in 'Highland Mary.' I think, Mr., Chairman, that the Minister of Public Works finds more ' divarsion ' in giving information he is not asked for than in answering the questions we put. He told us he was going to put the dredging in charge of some engineer in his department, but has it not always been in charge of an engineer?

Yes, but the chief engineer has had charge not only of dredging, but of general work connected with the department, and we have assigned this work to one whose special duty it will be to follow that work.

It is hardly worth while to lock the stable door after the horse is stolen. You should have made this appointment long ago. But why should you require the 34 clerks? Do you require them to look after this one engineer? I should like to ask the hon. minister, if it is his department which is doing the repairs to the post office at Halifax?
Yes.

How is it they are not finished? Last year I was told by thel

minister that the work was to be completed the 1st March, 1910, but that the contractor could not get it done in that time and consequently he had been given until the 1st of July. But the post office is not finished yet, and the contractor wrote the other day a letter to the Halifax ' Herald,' in which he said he had nothing to do with the delay at all, that it was, the fault of the department, because the department had sent down a lot of fittings which were perfectly useless and had to be returned.

The senior member for Halifax asked a question regarding that post office a few days ago, and my hon. friend will find the answer I gave in ' Hansard.' When we come to the item for the completion of that building will be the proper time to discuss it. I shall be glad then to give all possible information.

As the hon. minister did not give any satisfactory information regarding the number of extra clerks, I thought I would draw his attention to this post office, which is in very much the same condition as when it was started.
No.

All I can say is that from the outside it looks the same, and no one is allowed inside.
Department of Public Works-contingencies, $20,500.

There is an increase here of $5,000. This is in clerical and. other assistance. That is the amount estimated by the secretary of the department for additional assistance required of a temporary character. During the session we have to employ temporary clerks necessary to aid us in the making of returns for the House.
Department of Inland Revenue-salaries, $106,387.50.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
