There is a small increase here of about $2,000, due almost altogether to statutory increases. The number of employees is the same as last year. The inside staff remains the same, namely, 71 in number. The aggregate increase in the estimates of 1911-12 over 1910-11 is $2,175. Under departmental salaries there is one increase in the First Division subdivision B, which is caused by the intention of the department to promote the assistant secretary from Second Division Subdivision A to First Division Subdivision B. In the Second Division Subdivision A there is an increase of one, which, through the promotion of the assistant secretary from this class, enables the department to promote two clerks from the Second Dvision Subdivision B to the Second Division Subdivision A. In the Mr. CROSBY.
Second Division Subdivision B there is a decrease, which is caused by the intended promotion of two clerks from this grade to-a higher grade, and the promotion of one clerk from the next lower grade to this grade. In the Third Division, Subdivision A, there is an increase of one clerk, which is caused by the proposed promotion of one clerk to the class above and two clerks into 3-A from the class below. In the Third Division Subdivision B there is a decrease of two clerks promoted, as referred to above. The number of clerkships on departmental staff remains as in current estimates. In the laboratory branch the staff remains unchanged as respects numbers, but four of the assistant analysts it is the desire to promote from the Second Division Subdivision B to the Second Division Subdivision A. These gentlemen are technical officers and are well deserving of the promotion suggested. The Methylated Spirits Branch, the Electricity Branch ,and the Weights and Measures Branch remain unchanged as respects numbers and classification. The aggregate increase of $2,175, above referred to, is almost exclusively made up of annual increments.
Inland Revenue-contingencies, $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is no increase in this amount, but we have rearranged it a little. For last year we had $1,200 for clerical assistance, but did not require it all. For the coming year we reduce that to $700 and distribute the balance among stationery and sundries.
Department of Customs-salaries, $261,237.50.

I may give a general explanation, and then if hon. gentlemen desire to discuss any particular points they can be taken up for more detailed explanation. The principal cause of an increase of $16,262.50 in this vote is the proposed addition of 16 officers to the staff, 14 by appointment and two by transfer from the customs outside service. It is proposed to appoint twelve clerks in class 2-B at the minimum salary of $800, and to transfer two from the customs outside service to the same division at their present salaries of $1,200 and $950. One clerk is to be appointed in 3-B at the minimum salary of $500 and one messenger at a minimum of $500. The yearly salaries of these 16 officers will amount to $12,750. The commissioner considers the additional staff necessary on account of the increase of the work. The entries inward for the year 1908-9 numbered 1,072,863, for 1909-10 1,251,394, and for the six months of the current year 635,047. The custom revenue for the year 1908-9 was $48,059,791.93, for 1909-10 $61,919,622.42, and for the seven months of the current fiscal year $41,372,129.91. When the additional officers have been appointed seven will be assigned to the work in the statistical

branch, six will be' employed in checking entries, two as checkers and sorters, and one as messenger in the statistical branch. In these estimates, provision has been made lor statutory increases to all of the officers not at their maximum except two, and such statutory increases amount to $7,950. It is proposed to promote one officer from Division 1-B to Division 1-A, to promote one from 2-A to 1-B, and to promote two from 2-B to 2-A and one from 3-A to 2-B. These proposed payments account for an increase of $275 in the estimates. The increases for 1911-12 are therefore:-
Additions to the staff, 16 officers. $12,750
Statutory increases	 7,950
Promotions	 275
Total	  $20,975
A reduction in this amount of $4,712.50 has resulted from vacancies caused by deaths, resignations and transfers during the year being filled by appointments of officers at lower salaries, leaving a net proposed increase of $16,262.50.
The large increase in the work absolutely demands these increases in the staff. Comparing the estimates of this year with those of last year, sixteen officers seems a large number to add, but during the year we were not able to carry on the work with our regular staff and had to bring some of the outside officers here. They were paid out of the votes for the ports to which they were assigned and then out of contingencies we had to pay some temporary clerks supplied us by the Civil Service Commission, so that this is not really a jump of sixteen officers this year. We shall try to get along with this number but under contingencies we are asking for some $2,000 or $3,000 additional, out of which we will pay some extra clerks whom we will obtain from the Civil Service Commission. This year we were not able to give some of the clerks their three weeks' holidays.

We have heard a great deal of the extra work in the hon. gentleman's department. It seems to me that a considerable amount of that work has been brought about by the many changes in our tariff and the complications of the present tariff. We have a general tariff, a preferential tariff, an intermediate tariff, a French tariff, wnich applies to twelve or thirteen other countries, a Japanese tariff and I do not know how many others. Undoubtedly this must add greatly to the work in the department, and if we had a straight tariff readily understood I believe a clerk could do a great deal more work.
Yes, that is our experience, it has entailed more work in the department.
Does that account for a considerable proportion of the increased number of men wanted or are there other causes?

There are other causes. Of course as he suggests the different tariffs have greatly increased the statistical work and also the work in our check department but that does not account for all the increase. The revenue last year from customs was $10,000,000 greater than the year before and it looks as if the revenue this year would be $10,000,000 greater than that of last year. Then, the number of invoices, which is really what causes the work, rose from 1,072,863 in 1908-9 to 1,251,394 last year, while for the six months of the current year we have already 635,047 entries. The entries are increasing and the revenue is raising at the same rate.
Are these sixteen additional clerks all brought in from the outside service, all men of experience?
Oh, no, not all.
At what salary would new clerks without experience start?

They will go in at $800, the minimum of that class. It is proposed to promote Mr. F. O. Bennett, chief clerk of the statistics, from Subdivision ' B ' of the First Division to Subdivision ' A.' He is now at the maximum of his class, $2,800, and he will go into the minimum of the class above that, which is $2,800, the amount he now receives.
His statutory increases will go on again?
Yes, he is at a standstill now.
A magnificent scheme to get away with money.
When I tell you that Mr. Bennett is in charge of the compilation and publication of the Trade and Navigation returns and has ninety officers under his supervision and has thirty-nine years service

I think he is a very good man.
Mr. PATERSON

the House will agree
that he is worthy of promotion. To fill his place, and this is the only other promotion, we are promoting Mr. W. F. Wilson from 2-A to the division from which we moved Mr. Bennett, 1-B, at the minimum salary of $2,100. Mr. Wilson has been acting as inspector of preventive service since the death of Mr. F. L. Jones who had charge of that work. He has been in the service for seventeen years and is in charge of a very important branch of the work. Then,

provision is made for statutory increases of $100 each to the remaining eight officers in the service, making $800 in all. That is the class in which you can give an increase of $100. In the lower class statutory increases are only $50, and so on. These places have to be filled, but it necessitates bringing in twelve new men and it is proposed to start them at the minimum of the class from $800 to $1,600.
Will these twelve new men come in on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission?

Yes. The fact of the matter is that the department does not appoint new officers at all. The Civil Service Commission appoint the men. When we find that we want a man the commission has to notify him that there is a vacancy, they give the name of the man and the fact of their giving the name appoints him. We do not have to put an order in council through appointing him. After he has been there for six months, if he should prove incapable of discharging the duties of the office the commissioner of the department may notify'the Civil Service Commissioners that the officer they gave him seems to be not able for the work and the Civil Service Commissioners will have to give him another name. So, the services of that officer would be dispensed with and the man who succeeds him would be appointed bv nomination of the Civil Service Commission. It is in their hands now.
Does the minister intend to apply that principle to the outside service?

That is worthy of consideration, and it would relieve the minister very much if we were able to have that established in some of the large ports. But I have not been able just to determine how that might be done. Of course, you can see it would not be practicable in many cases in the smaller offices. If we ask for a man to fill a position in the inside service he can come from any province, but in many of the local offices it would not work so well, because people would not want to leave their homes. The salaries would not warrant them in moving, and it might be that in some of these ports, for instance, in one of the hon. gentleman's own ports, he would not want somebody to be brought from away off at a distance because he had happened to pass a better qualifying examination. The local men may be as capable for the duties, but they may not have passed the literary examination. But, if we could devise something of that kind in the very large ports it would take a great deal of the work and thought off the minister.
Are we to understand that the minister seriously contemplates having the appointments made in the larger ports of entry under the Civil Service Commission?

You must not understand me as being committed to it, because I have not studied it out sufficiently to see how it might work and what difficulties there might be in the way. The thought has been in my mind, but I have not arrived at any conclusion further than the natural conclusion that the minister is relieved of the responsibility for appointments which is placed upon the Civil Service Commission, and it is supposed as a result of the examination they hold that the men they name are capable for the positions. Do not understand me as being pledged to that. I think it would, perhaps, be easier for me, but there may be great difficulties in the way of doing it.

What additional conveniences and accommodation is the minister giving to the people in the way of ports of entry and outports in view of the large increase in the imports into the country? Is the minister increasing the number of ports?

Yes, we are. We are going as slow as we can, but going that slow even, the demands are so great, especially in the northwest, and their cases are so strong that when we come to the general item you will find that I am going to ask for $100,000 more, part of which must go towards opening up some new outports in our growing country, and I do hope that outside of that we will have enough to give a slight addition to very many of the outside officers who are giving us faithful service and who maintain that at the present time their salaries are insufficient to give them such a living as they are fairly entitled to.

While the government is receiving a great revenue through the customs in Halifax and St. John half our customs officers there axe working at a salary below $1,000 a year. I feel that the time has come when, in ports like Halifax and St. John, where there is a great traffic going through all the time, and where you require the services of responsible men, there should not be one officer receiving less than $1,000. Under the conditions which exist to-day it is impossible for a man to live in a city and to maintain himself in such a position as that which a customs officer should occupy on the salaries that they are receiving. I hope that when the Minister of Customs brings down his estimates with regard to the outside service he will see that our officers in these poTts, where there is a large immigra-

tion going through and a large amount of customs work to be done night and day, axe more adequately compensated. I hope he may be able to make the minimum salary in the Customs Department not less than $1,000.

While I sympathize with the officers, I do hope that the hon. gentleman will not let the idea go out and be entertained by the officers outside that we are going to establish a minimum of $1,000. A hundred thousand dollars would be nowhere if we attempted that. We are trying to give each man who is not at what we consider' the maximum now about $50 a year. Three years ago I took $150,000, and then $100,000 next year, but if you begin to spread that from the Atlantic to the Pacific it becomes very thin foT each one. I would hesitate to ask parliament to give me enough money to do that, though 1 might have the same opinion that my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) has about it. But don't let the idea get* abroad that the minimum salary of our outside officers should be $1,000, because that would be an impossibility. I would not raise such hope as that, because it cannot be gratified.
I do not want it to apply to the whole of the outside service.
Only to Halifax, I suppose.

We have just voted $357,000 in one lump for the inside service in Ottawa, and I am not complaining about it. but the minister must know that people in other parts of Canada find it just as hard to live, and are just as good livers, if they have the opportunity, as they are in Ottawa. You have very few competent men in the customs department in Ottawa, who are. not getting more than $1,000 a year; you take a man into the inside service today, and he commencs with a salary of $900, and yet you have competent men in the city of Halifax who have been for 20 years in the customs department, and you only pay them $800 a year. I have nothing at all to say against the men in the inside service; I believe there are good men in that service, but I do say that they are not a bit better than the men in the outside service. In the outside customs service in Halifax,-where travel is going through all the time, and where but for the efficiency and honesty of your officers, the customs revenue would be very much less,-and you are not compensating your men properly. I know the minister has done fairly well since he came to the department in the matter of salaries, but progress has been slow and when you find customs officers in Halifax who have been 25 years in the service, and who get less than $800 a year, I say it is not fair play. I ask for consideration for
these men, and I am sure the minister will try to do the best he can so that if he cannot bring them up to $1,000 a year, he will bring them pretty close to it.
Would the Minister of Customs approve or disapprove of officers of his department taking active part in election campaigns?
Taking an active part in election campaigns?
Yes.
Oh, no, I would discourage anything of the kind.

I wish to get the minister's views upon ' Hansard ', because I think it is well that his opinion should be understood by officers of his department. I am informed that one of his officers, a gentleman who had something in the nature of a roving commission, took a very active part in an election in Nova Scotia not very long ago. And while I do not wish to make any charge against the man in question, and I am not doing so, I wish to get the minister's views recorded in ' Hansard ' so that it may perhaps have a salutory effect.

I do not remember that any complaint of that kind has reached me. In some cases, a community may wish to elect a customs officer as councillor or school trustee, and we are asked about it, and our answer is, that our officers had better not occupy any of these positions. It might not conflict with their work, but even in municipal elections there is feeling aroused and as our officers have to deal with the public, we discourage anything of that kind. There have been cases in which there was a unanimous desire that one of our officers should serve the public in such a capacity, but we thought it better that he should not do so, and we try to keep them in line if we can.

The gentleman to whom I refer, was in no sense a candidate, he was not asked to be a candidate, he was not personally interested in the election, I am informed that he was not even a voter in the constituency in which the election was being held.
Was it a municipal election?
No, it was an election for the legislature of Nova Scotia, and I simply wish to have the minister's view on ' Hansard,' and I am glad to find he is opposed to any such thing.

I had intended at a later period of the session, to discuss a similar matter, but now that the subject is broached, I will speak to it. The minister says that he endeavours to keep his

officers in line if he can. I do not understand the meaning of that expression. Does he mean to say that it is impossible for him to keep the employees of his department out of political contests?
Do you mean with reference to their running for office?
I mean with reference to their taking an active part in politics. Is it impossible for the minister to keep the employees of his department out of active politics.
I think we do, so far as I know.

Then I will ask the minister this. If I submit indisputable evidence to the Minister of Customs that employees of his department are taking an active part in political campaigns, will he dismiss them?
We will have to be guided by the circumstances of the case.
That is a very different thing altogether.

Is the hon. gentleman now speaking of Dominion elections or is he speaking of provincial and municipal elections . I make a distinction between municipal and Dominion elections, but I say that even in municipal elections it is desirable that our officers should not take an active part. The officer may contend that in a municipal election he has a direct interest as he is a taxpayer and the question before the municipality is whether they will go into a large public expenditure, and that he has a right to concern himself in that, but I say in a general way we dissuade our officers from making themselves in any way offensive or even active in a municipal election.

I will put a concrete case, and although I will not give the name of the man, it is an actual case. This man is the treasurer of the political organization in a district in my constituency; he is also perhaps the most active political worker in the district; he is municipal councillor for the district and the municipal contests there are run upon strict party lines; he is the man who collects the party campaign contributions in his district, and he stands at the polling booth on election day. His name appears in the press as being an officer of this political association, and I am prepared to substantiate these facts by affidavit. In such a case would the minister regard that man as sufficiently partisan to dismiss him from the department?
Is he an officer of Customs?
Yes.
I would be very pleased if the hon. gentleman would give me the facts and I will consider the case.

Of course the minister would be pleased to consider it but what I ask him now is if he would regard these circumstances as causing him to think that man sufficiently partisan to be dismissed from the service.	.
The hon. gentleman puts a hypothetical case.
No, this is an actual case and I will give the proof later on.
When the facts come before me I will be able to answer it.

But I want a declaration from the minister now because I do not want to waste his time or mine by getting affidavits and preparing data and then have the matter discussed^ at a later stage I want to know from the minister how far his officers can go in political controversy down in our province. I may tell him that politics is rampant among officials in Nova Scotia, and we have had to contend against it year after year so that it is well to know where we are going to draw the line. If the minister fails now to give me a positive direct answer I will have the matter discussed at a later stage when the data will be in better shape.
That would be better.
I wish also to put an actual case before the Minister of Customs. Would the minister approve of one of his officers being a licensed hotel keeper in a village?
No, I would not approve of it.

In view of the remarks made by the hon. Minister of Customs, I think we are entitled to an answer to the question put by my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes). The Minister of Customs stated very distinctly that he thought it would * be very wrong for an officer of his department to take part in politics, even in municipal politics. Then my hon. friend asked him : ' If I present you with a case where an officer of your department takes an active part in pslitics, municipal or otherwise, what will you do?' Then he begins to hedge and beat about the bush. When my hon. friend presents a straight case, exactly in line with what the minister said, he asks time to consider, he will have to know the man and know all about him.

The hon. gentleman can take that view of it if he likes ; but the hon. gentleman has presented this case, being a lawyer, would, I think, admit that

my position was not unreasonable, that I should know the facts of the case 'before I pronounced upon it.

In that respect I am quite prepared to take the attitude of the minister, at the same time, I think this House should know, and I propose that at some time during the session we shall know, what the hon. minister's policy is to be with respect to his employees becoming interested in political contests. I think that should be known both in the interest of efficient service and in the interest of the men themselves. On that point I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat.
The hon. gentleman is willing to wait until I ascertain the facts?
Surely.

I think a great deal depends on the amount of salary an officer gets. If he is in a town or city and gets a living salary, he should devote himself wholly to the duties of his office. But there are hundreds of men who are engaged perhaps as preventive officers at $50 or $100 a year. Would you expect a man to retire from municipal politics and from active interest in public matters in his own district because he gets that small sum? I think that consideration ought to govern in a great many instances.

I understand that the hon. member for Guysborough has put a question to me. I do not know that I am called on to answer it, but I wish to be perfectly fair. What I wish to find out is what the policy of the department is- how far its employees are to be permitted to mix in politics. My hon. friend asks me if I think that men receiving small salaries should not be allowed to take.part in public matters. I say yes, if they are conducted on party lines. But the difficulty is that these offices in the smaller districts of Nova Scotia are dangled as plums before the eyes of the party workers; that I know ; and they have to get up and hustle for their party in order to get them. Active political partisanship counts for more than efficiency. That is the crux of the whole difficulty, and the sooner we root politics entirely out of the service the more efficient it will become. I do not speak thus in any narrow, partisan sense. I dare say the same thing may have occurred before 1896 ; I am prepared to admit that for the sake of argument. But I do not want hon. gentlemen opposite to quote that in justification of themselves. We ought to rise above that sort of thing and deal with the situation of the moment; and if we do we shall have a far more efficient public service throughout this country.

I am very glad the hon. member for Guysborough has raised the question of the distinction between those officers of the 'Customs Department employed in the rural districts and those who receive sufficient salary to compensate them for all their time. He holds that a person acting as a preventive officer in a rural district and receiving a pittance of $50 a year should not be debarred from entering municipal politics, but that an officer in a city receiving a substantial salary should devote the whole of his time to his official duties. I would like to remind the hon. Minister of Customs that in the municipal elections in Cape Breton, in 1904, Mr. Ratchford, the collector at Victoria Mines, who receives I think $80 a year, was nominated as a candidate, and there came a letter signed by the hon. Minister of Customs to the Collector of Customs at Sydney, the late Mr. Macdonald, directing that this man either withdraw his candidature or resign his office. Less than two years ago, Mr. Fitzgerald, of the city of Sydney, who receives $800 or $900 a year, and who is presumed to devote a great deal of time to the duties of his office, was nominated as an aider-man of the city of Sydney. I myself drew this to the attention of the minister, yet Mr. Fitzgerald continued as a candidate, and he sits to-day at the council board of the city of Sydney. If there is any equity in this matter, it would seem that the collector at Victoria Mines should not have been interfered with in becoming a municipal councillor, while there would have been some justice in debarring Mr. Fitzgerald from being an aldermanic candidate. What I would like to have from the hon. minister, for the benefit of the officers and the public, is whether there is any rule in this matter or whether it is intended to have a hard and fast rule. In the one instance, the man was a Tory and was not allowed to run for municipal honours because it was not desirable that the council should be Conservative. The other man was a Liberal and he was allowed to run. I do not think the minister should blow hot and cold in a matter of this kind. If Mr. Fitzgerald can run as an alderman I do not know why another man should not equally run as alderman. I would like to know from the minister what he intends to do with regard to these office-holders. Are they eligible for municipal office or not?

There was a circular issued from the department years before I became head of it, in which the attention of the officers was called to the fact that it was undesirable they should take any active part in politics, or hold any corporate office. I do not remember that 1904 case at all, but I presume that when attention was called to it the same course was followTed



in that as in every other vase. I do not know whether such a letter was sent in 1904 to this gentleman, who may have been a Conservative in his leanings; but the hon. gentleman will surely take my word when I say that when the attention of the department is drawn to any such case a letter is written to the party complained against inclosing the memorandum I have mentioned. There was a case where the party had served some years, but finally our attention was called to it, when half the year was through, and he wrote back saying he would like to finish out the year. We have had from the Niagara district both political parties and the municipal authorities urging us to waive the provision in so far as it referred to a trustee whose services they considered very valuable, but I know of no instance in which, when the matter was brought to our notice, we did not send this memorandum, and I fancy it has always had the desired effect. There are, of course, some hard cases. There was one the other day, I think. A man who gets $100 was asked to run for some little office which would give him $25. My personal sympathies were all with him, but his case was brought before us and a letter was sent to him with the circular, and he wrote back saying he was sorry, but he would not run for the $25 office. In fudging such cases one does not want to be too hard.
This is all very pathetic.
And very true.

But what we want to find out is on what principle the department acts. I am not saying they should exclude every one, although I believe that all departmental officers should be prevented in taking an active part in political contests. You have no difficulty in filling the offices. As a rule there are 15 applicants for every office, even down to a $25 one. But can there not be some line drawn beyond which no man, Liberal or Conservative, can go. If the hon. minister will say that every man with a salary under $100 may take an active part in a political contest we shall know what to expect. It is all very well to send circulars and remonstrate, but if the minister were engaged in a manufacturing enterprise and he did not choose that his employees should smoke on the premises he would not send circulars or remonstrances, but he would say: You will not smoke on the premises or you will be dismissed.
The line is very clearly drawn. A public officer has a perfect right to vote, but he is not allowed to do anything offensive in connection with any election.

I believe that every man ought to vote. In fact, I think there should be legislation taking away the franchise Mr. PATERSON.
from the man who does not vote unless he can show good reasons for keeping away from the poll. But that is not the point. I have been using the word ' active partisanship,' and that is what I want to get at.
That is not favoured.

In the ease I brought to the attention of the committee Mr. Ratch-ford, who received a small salary was stopped from being a candidate in the manner I have described because, when the notice was sent him he withdrew his nomination. In the other case in which the minister assures me he wrote in the same wav, that of Mr. Fitzgerald, he did not withdraw his nomination. All this discussion goes for nothing unless the minister will admit that the regulation is so loosely drawn that it frightens a Tory away from a nomination, while a Grit does not need to care a hang for it. If that be the case, the regulation should be re-drawn; it should make it clear either that a man has a right to run or that he has no right to run. Merely to write to a candidate and inclose a circular to the effect that the department thinks it undesirable that one in its employ should be a candidate for municipal honours will not do, and I have pointed out these instances to show that it does not do, -that, as I have said, it frightens a Tory away from a nomination but encourages a Grit to go on. I ask the minister if he thinks that equitable? If not, will he undertake to have the regulation so amended as either to leave either party free to run or to make it clear that neither party may run? They ought to be put on an equal footing-Grit and Tory, large-salaried man or small-salaried man. I do not see that the salary should make a great deal of difference one way or the other. I ask the minister for his opinion about the matter. And, if he thinks the regulation is not fair, will he have one drafted that will be fair?

So far as the notice is concerned, I have already stated that it is sent in every case that is brought to my official knowledge-the same circular accompanied by a letter calling the party's attention to it.

I quite agree that the regulation is sent. But it is the regulation I am criticising. If this goes from the minister to a prospective candidate w-ho is a Tory, that candidate trembles in his boots and resigns; but, if a Grit, he does not have to. The candidate is not told that if he persists his office will be declared vacant or that he will be subject to any other penalty. And so, I ask the minister if he thinks the regulation is fair, and, if not, will he undertake to have a regulation drawn up that will either leave it open to

all these people to become candidates or debar them all alike?

I do liot think that the fact that a man receives a salary of $100 ought to disqualify him from any position. If he is to be disqualified from engaging in any other business, because he has a government position, that government position should afford him a living. I go further and say that the mere fact of running for the office of municipal councillor should not be regarded as taking an active part in politics. It is a sad fact that there are politics in municipal councils in counties and in towns as well. But it should not be so, and I do not think that this drawing of party lines in municipal affairs should be assisted by the department by regarding the fact of a man engaging in a municipal election as an act of political partisanship. I understand that my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) has quoted the case of Ratchford and Carrol, an election that took place in the county of Cape Breton some three years ago. One would imagine that this was a contest between Ratchford as a Tory and Carrol as a Grit, and that Ratchford the Tory got frightened and retired from the conflict. I do not know whether the hon. member said that in the first instance or not, but I gather from his observations now that that is what he wanted the committee to understand-that Ratchford was a Tory and was scared away from the contest, and Carrol, a Grit, was permitted to go in by acclamation. I am a much older man in the county of Cape Breton than my hon. friend. I know Mr. Ratchford well, have known him for twenty-five years, and know that during that time he has been a straightforward, consistent supporter of the Liberal party, and that he was appointed to office by this government. Now, why he should get scared by a notice from this government who appointed him and were friendly to him and should avoid the responsibility of running, I do not quite understand. Mr. Ratchford and Mr. Carrol were both Liberals and both supporting the Liberal warden. Whichever of the two came into the council, it did not make the slightest difference to the Liberal party, so I do not see what advantage it would be to the government to frighten away one or the other. So, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) is making a point of the fact that we were scaring Ratchford away and trying to get Carrol in, he will fail in making that point with anybody who knows the facts. As to partisanship in this matter, so far as the department is concerned, I know of the case of a gentleman in North Cape Breton, who ran for the council this year. I suppose the man opposing him a strong Conservative partisan thought to drive him out of the field by notifying the department. So 34i
the other man, who was a Liberal, received the notification. Well, he was strong enough to stand to his guns, ran the election and put the Tory out of business. He is the councillor for the district, whatever may happen. But, as I have said, I contend that the mere fact of a man running for municipal office should not be regarded as an act of partisanship.

I do not pretend to know so much about the political complexion, of the electors of Cape Breton county as the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) who has just spoken. However, I made acquaintance with a sufficient number of the Conservative faith to find a seat in this House. Perhaps the minister was quite familiar with the politics of Mr. Ratchford, of South Bar. All he has said about his politics may be true. I do not say he was scared away from the candidature, but I say he received a notification from the Minister of Customs after he had canvassed the district, after he was nominated, and he retired from the contest. I was not arguing against the right of a collector of customs to run for municipal honours but I am arguing against the inefficiency and the unfairness of this regulation. The member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has simply put forth an argument along the same line's as I have been advocating this week. He has demonstrated another instance of the absolute inefficiency of the Act. He cited a case where a Liberal office holder received a notification from the Minister of Customs but was strong enough to stand to his guns. Think what strength it required for a Grit Customs officer to stand to his guns with such an elastic notification as that. Why should there exist a regulation to be mailed at all to any man employed in the Customs Department when he seeks municipal political honours unless that notification means something, unless it means that he is to be encouraged or discouraged in his candidature, that he is permitted to run or is prohibited from running. Such a regulation should carry with it some penalty, either of dismissal, suspension or fine. Personally I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie).
I know no good reason why this man should not be permitted to run, but there should be no regulation which, wlifcn sent to one man will have the effect of causing him to withdraw and when sent to another will permit him to run. I am not discussing the policy of permitting or not permitting Customs officers to become candidates; my point is that this regulation can be directed to one man and cause Rim to withdraw while another man can stand to his guns as the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) has pointed out. So I return to

the question which I submit to the minister, does he think a regulation of that kind is effective, that it will work out equitably? If it does not, will he undertake to have a regulation drawn that will either leave the field open to these men or close it to them, Grit and Tory alike?

I do not know that 1 understand the hon. gentleman. We deal with all cases when they come before us in precisely the same way. What the effect may be I do not know. The effect ought to be that when an officer received that communication he would know that the department did not favour his running. It does not necessarily follow that political feeling is aroused, for, as has been said, there are many contests in which the line between Liberal and Conservative is utterly obliterated. I do not know Whether the man is a Liberal or a Conservative. If the charge comes before us that So and So, one of our officers, is going to run in this or that municipality, we write a letter to him calling his attention to this circular which we inclose What he may do after I cannot say, that is with himself. If charges are made to me that this circular is disregarded, then we may have some further communication with him. While that circular may not go the length of saying to a man: If you run for that office you will be dismissed, it does warn then that the department do not favour and would endeavour to discourage his running. In a municipal contest feeling may run just as high as in a political contest, and we do not want our officers to take an active part in matters of that kind which would render them not pleasing to the community as a whole in discharging their duties as Customs officers; we want to have our officers in such relations with the community that every man, whatever his political opinion may be, will go and transact the public business with him with a feeling of friendliness to him. It may be in the interest of the municipality to have our officers hold a, municipal position, but if, by his candidature, feeling is aroused against him among a section of the community, then we consider it is not in the interest of the department. We have only one line of conduct towards all officers. The hon. gentleman knows, for he will do me the credit, surely of believing my word, that I told him when he spoke to me of this case, that we did not approve of such a course and that we would communicate with the officer at once. We did communicate with the officer, and we would communicate with any officer in a similar position whose case was brought to our attention.

I am quite prepared to believe that the minister is prepared to deal Mr. MADDIN.
in the one way with every case which comes before him, be the subject a Liberal, or a Liberal-Conservative. What I am endeavouring to find out is what that one way is. As a candidate I do not care whether a man runs for a municipal office or not, it does not matter to me politically. Since the matter has been discussed, I believe it is a mistake to have a man run even for the position of municipal councillor if he is a customs officer. These men have to do with the passing of goods. They may wish to increase their strength in the community, and there may be one or two men who buy goods, and whose political favour they would like to have, and, being human, it is natural to suppose that if any favours can be granted by these officers, to these men they will grant them. Being human, it is very natural to suppose that if any favours can be granted to the customs officer he is going to receive them. As so often happens in small communities, he is also the merchant, and a man who has goods to take through that office will take care that he will buy his goods of the man who has the customs office in his own shop. That is a reason, I think, why these men should not mix in municipal contests,.whether political contests or not. The only point I wish to raise, and I do not raise it in a partisan way at all, is that I wish to find out what measure to apply to these men. I will do the minister the justice to believe that he will apply the rule the same to a. Liberal as to a Conservative if I can find out what the rule is. I put an actual, concrete case to him in which the customs officer is the treasurer and secretary of the Liberal organization in his district. He is named in advertisements in the press as being the treasurer, he attends the meetings of the party, stands outside the poll on election day, and is perhaps the most active man in the district in the Liberal interest in every contest, either Dominion or provincial. I could not get the minister to commit himself to saying that if I could prove the facts he will dismiss that man. I am trying to find out how far a man can go who is a customs officer and still retain his position.
We certainly will look into the case if the hon. gentleman brings it before us.
The Minister of Customs tells us that he wishes to be very fair in this matter.
Not very fair-just equitable.

He says that he appeals to my fairness and assures me that he sent a copy of this circular to Mr. Fitzgerald after I complained a year ago that he was a candidate. I unquestionably accept his statement, but that brings me back to the

point: What is the use of this regulation?
I asked the minister three consecutive times, and he could very plainly answer * yes ' or ' no whether he thinks that regulation is effective. Is it the purpose of the department to prevent their officers taking part in municipal contests? If it is their intention he must see that the regulation is utterly worthless. In the instance that I have reference to Mr. Fitzgerald continued as the candidate notwithstanding the communication received from the department, and he sits at the council board as he has a right to do. The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) instanced another case within a few weeks, and the man stood by his guns. There are two specific instances demonstrating the absolute worthlessness of this regulation, if it is a regulation to prohibit customs officers from entering municipal politics. Since the minister would not answer my question as to whether he would draw up a new and effective regulation, would he take us into his confidence to-night and tell us what he proposes to do with regard to the two officers who did not obey the instructions in the circular, who did not accept his counsel, who stood by their guns, and treated it with contempt? What is he going to do in future cases which may arise of a similar character?
Does the hon. gentleman prefer that charge now?

I do not propose to charge any man with doing anything he has a right to do. I am pointing out that the regulation does not provide any penalty against Mr. Fitzgerald for running. It does not make it an offence for any man to run. So, what charge is there to make? The circular says that the department think it undesirable that any officer should enter into municipal contests or hold office under corporations. What charge could you lay under a regulation of that kind? What tribunal could you lay it before? I suppose I could go to the minister's office some afternoon, and say:	There is one of your
customs officers who, notwithstanding the fact that you issued a circular, still insisted on running for the municipal council, and sits there; what are you going to do about it?
I would write to the officer and say that a complaint had been made against him.

Would that constitute a charge? It is a mere statement of the fact as it exists, and it is not for the purpose of finding fault with that officer that I am making this protest here to-night. It is to demonstrate to the minister that this regulation is utterly worthless and useless,
and is only sent out when occasion demands it for a certain purpose. It has the-effect of driving an undesirable candidate from the field, from the Tory point of view,, while a Grit candidate can stand by his-guns and laugh at it. I do not wish to lay a charge against any officer of the Department of Customs. The worthlessness of this regulation has been demonstrated by the testimony of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, and by the instance which I have cited here and I ask the minister what he is going to do about it? Is he going to retain that worthless circular and mail it out to his officers in the country when municipal elections come on, or is he going to meet the situation face to face and make a new and effective regulation? What does the minister say?
I think I have said all I need say.
I would ask if he intends to draft a new regulation that will be effective? Will he or will he not?

I prefer the regulation as it is, for the reason that I have explained. We do not approve, in fact, we discourage .cases such as that which the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), has pointed out. We would rather that our customs officers did not engage in anything in which feeling in the community might be aroused, not that it is a sin for a man to occupy a position in the municipal council. It may be for the benefit of the community, but the object of the department-and this was, no doubt, the view which was taken when the order was issued, which was long before I came into the department-is to let the officer see that the government did not approve of it, that they thought it was altogether better that, while serving the public in a public capacity, for all men have to do business with them, they should not engage in any contest in which feeling might be aroused over some municipal or political question. We do think that our officers, when they receive that, recognize from it that the view of the department is against that, and if there be a case or two where they have disregarded it-the hon. gentleman mentions a case now, and there have been others mentioned-I think I would be safe in saying that they are the only two that have been brought to my notice in so far as I know, one of them only to-night, indicating that it has had its effect. It may not have had its effect somewhere else, but I have heard nothing of it; so that, it cannot be said that it is ineffective. It is very effective. We do not think that we should absolutely prohibit it-that is another question,-but when a complaint is made to us that circular is sent with a letter to the

officer, calling his attention to it which indicates what the mind of the department is with reference to it.

Surely that rule of the department should have some penalty attached to it for non-compliance. The minister says that first of all, he fires a shot at the officer, by sending him that notice, and if he does not comply with it, he sends another shot at him. But, what happens if the officer still stands on his ground, and says to him:	I do not care for your notice; I am going to stay on the job?
We have never had to fire a second shot yet.
Let the minister make a plain statement now as to what he will do to a man who persistently disregards the advice of the department, and he will save a great deal of future trouble.
We will tell him that we want him to mind what we tell him.
And send him another letter.
And if he disobeys again what will the minister do?
We will try and do what we think is right, as the hon. gentleman himself would do.

If the minister will state now that he will dismiss such an officer it will save trouble, and that officer ?ar*' *n Political campaigns hereafter. My hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) nas cited a case where a customs officer is secretary-treasurer of the Liberal Association and advertised in the papers as such, and stands at the polling booth on election day, and surely the minister can say that such a man is not entitled to be in his department. If the minister says that now, many a customs officer throughout the country will take heed. A few years ago a resolution was passed by the House emphatically stating that no official should take part in elections under pain of forfeiture of office, but that resolution is ignored. Personally I do not object to an official going into a municipal election, but that an officer of the Crown, paid by the people, should use his duties not on behalf of the people but on behalf of one political party, ought not to be tolerated.
If the hon. gentleman from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) places the information before me reciting these facts, I shall do as I have done in other cases.
Send them a letter?

I will send them this letter, I will say that certain charges, naming them, have been preferred against you and I want your answer to them, and the answer comes , and then I shall judge as to future action. Do not think that we are novices in this business.
We know you are not.

There have beep charges upon charges preferred against officers, and we have asked the man for his defence and we have judged on the merits of each case. If the hon. gentleman thinks that a man who takes a more active part in an election than he ought to, on the Conservative side, is dismissed because he happens to be a Conservative, he is attributing to the department what has not been the course of the department.

I do not want the minister to misinterpret me. I have never suggested that. I have repeatedly said this evening that I do believe that the Minister of Customs would deal equitably with each case. But I am trying to find out the measure he uses in dealing with these cases. I am not concerned about the poor Tory office holder because there are not very many of them left. I want to know from the Minister how far an official who takes an active part in political contests in my county can legitimately go. It has become notorious with us, so much so that I felt it almost useless to make any representation to the government, but when the question arose to-night I thought I would ask the minister whether such a case as this was not in flagrant violation of his own regulations. I am prepared to say now that I do not charge the minister with partisanship, because I have no evidence to that effect.

I candidly say that while I do not approve of this thing, I do not care to dismiss officers if I can help it. But if our officers do violate these rules we must have them dealt with. I must say that I do believe in giving an officer a chance to make a reply to charges.
Certainly.

And when he has made that reply, I deal with it. There have not been many cases brought to my notice in which a Liberal office-holder has been charged with being active in politics, but there have been a great many cases brought to my attention when our Conservative office-holders have been so charged. I suppose that if I were to listen to friends behind me their opinion would be that I had been very very lenient in

these eases. I like to give a man liberty, so much as I can, to take an interest inpublic affairs.
Hear, hear.
But the line is drawn at his having the right to vote and of speaking with people and discussing public questions with them as he may.
That is all right.

But for a man occupying a position in the customs, to be actively identified with a party, and active and offensive as the hon. gentleman says' this official is, that is a thing the department does not approve of, and the department will endeavour to deal with the case in some way when the hon. gentleman has laid the facts before me, and I have obtained the answer of the officer.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the House adjourned at 10.55 p.m.

Monday, December 12, 1910.
